# Performance and queueing {#sec-performance-and-queueing}

A server that can do $2000$ requests per second does not answer $1900$ requests per second in the same time as $100$.
Requests that arrive while it is busy wait, and the wait grows without bound as the load approaches the capacity. The
estimates of [Estimation and the design process](../estimation-and-the-design-process/index.qmd) chose a planned
utilisation, $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$, without saying what the remaining $40\%$ buys; this chapter says it. Its claims are of
three kinds. The quantities a designer measures (response time, throughput, percentiles, utilisation) and the two ways
in which load reaches a system (open and closed) are definitions. The results that relate them are theorems and
propositions with complete proofs: how many samples a percentile needs, Little's law, the M/M/1 and M/M/c queues with
the Erlang C formula, and the operational bounds of a closed system with their knee. Two facts of the theory of Markov
processes that the queueing results rest on, that the number of requests in an M/M/1 or M/M/c queue is a birth-death
process and that Poisson arrivals see time averages, are stated as quoted from their source.

The main source is @zukerman2013introduction, which states and derives every queueing result used here; where its
derivation is informal, as for Little's law, the chapter gives a complete proof. Tail latency follows @dean2013tail and
@dean2004mapreduce [Sec. 3.6]. The practice follows the benchmark books, none of which treats queueing quantitatively:
@tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Ch. 3], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 2], @pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024
[Ch. 7] and @gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 12]. The probability comes from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd), and the
birth-death processes from [Random processes](../../complexity-science/random-processes/index.qmd) in Complexity Science.

The chapter has five sections. @sec-latency-throughput defines response time, throughput, percentiles and utilisation,
and proves how many samples estimate a percentile. @sec-littles-law proves Little's law. @sec-mm1 defines the Poisson
process and derives the M/M/1 queue. @sec-mmc derives the M/M/c queue and the Erlang C formula and uses them to plan
capacity. @sec-open-closed defines open and closed systems and proves the bounds that locate the knee of a load test.

The running example is again the photo-sharing service (@exm-req-workload-assumptions): its feed receives $1.74 \times
10^5$ requests per second at the peak, an application server serves $\mu = 2000$ requests per second, and the previous
chapters sized the pool at $146$ servers (@exm-load-servers).

Every definition, theorem and proposition is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden
solution in two tabs: the argument, then a computation with its recorded output. The computations run in plain Python
3.12 with NumPy, the standard library and, for the discrete-event simulations of queues, SimPy 4.1.2, always with fixed
seeds. Diagrams are written in the D2 language. Code that would need a running service, such as a load test, is marked
as illustrative and is not run.

## Latency, throughput and percentiles {#sec-latency-throughput}

Tan calls performance "the time taken for a user's request to the system to return a response" and lists as typical
targets "tens of milliseconds to several seconds" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.4, p. 65]. Requirements are stated
as percentiles of that time (@exm-req-latency-quantile), and Dean and Barroso explain why the high percentiles are the
hard part: "Multiple layers of queueing in intermediate servers and network switches amplify this variability"
[@dean2013tail, p. 76]. This section fixes the quantities that are measured on a running system (response time,
throughput, the empirical distribution and its percentiles, utilisation) and proves how many measurements a percentile
needs before it can be trusted. The rest of the chapter predicts these quantities from the arrival rate and the service
rate.

For more on this topic, see @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 3.4], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 2, "Latency"],
@dean2013tail [pp. 74-77] and @zukerman2013introduction [Secs. 3.2 and 4.1].

### Response time, throughput and utilisation

A measurement of a running system is a list of requests, each with the time it arrived and the time it was answered.
Everything a performance report contains is computed from that list and from the times the servers were busy. The
definition says how.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-response-time}
#### Response time, throughput, percentiles and utilisation

Let a system be observed over $[0, \Delta]$, and let request $i$ arrive at time $a_i$ and complete at time $d_i \geq a_i$.

1. The **response time** of request $i$ is $T_i = d_i - a_i$. The **arrival rate** over the window is the number of
   arrivals divided by $\Delta$, and the **throughput** $X$ is the number of completions divided by $\Delta$. The
   **capacity** of the system is the largest throughput it can sustain.
2. For $n$ measured response times with order statistics $T_{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq T_{(n)}$, the **empirical
   distribution function** is $\hat F_n(t) = \#\{i : T_i \leq t\}/n$, and the **empirical $q$-quantile** is $\hat t_q =
   T_{(\lceil qn\rceil)}$, the smallest measured time $t$ with $\hat F_n(t) \geq q$. It estimates the quantile $t_q$ of the
   response time's distribution. The **tail latency** is $t_q$ for $q$ close to one: the $99$th percentile (p99) $t_{0.99}$,
   the p99.9 $t_{0.999}$.
3. The **utilisation** of a server over the window is the fraction of $[0, \Delta]$ during which it is serving a request,
   and that of a pool of servers is the average of its servers' utilisations [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.2,
   p. 107].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Tan's definition of latency includes the network. Item 1 measures whatever interval the observer chooses.

::: {#exm-lat-tan}
#### What latency includes

Tan's latency "includes the network latency of the request to leave the client and travel to the service, the time the
service takes to process the request and create the response, and the network latency of the response"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.4, p. 65]. Measured at the client, $a_i$ and $d_i$ are the client's send and receive
times; measured at the server, they are its receipt and send times, and the network's round trips of
[The web stack](../the-web-stack/index.qmd) are excluded. A report must say which.
:::

The words for rates are used loosely. Tan separates two of them.

::: {#exm-lat-tan-bandwidth}
#### Throughput and capacity

"The maximum request rate that a system can process is its bandwidth. Throughput is the current request rate being
processed by the system. However, it is common (though incorrect) to use the term 'throughput' in place of 'bandwidth'"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Ch. 3, p. 55]. Tan's bandwidth is the capacity of item 1. A feed server of capacity $2000$
requests per second that receives $1200$ has throughput $1200$, until the arrival rate exceeds $2000$; then throughput
stays at $2000$ and the excess accumulates.
:::

The mean and the percentiles answer different questions. A small fraction of slow requests moves the mean little and the
high percentiles completely.

::: {#exm-lat-mean-vs-tail}
#### Mean and tail

If $99\%$ of $10\,000$ requests take $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $1\%$ take $1\,\mathrm{s}$, the mean is $0.99 \times 20 + 0.01
\times 1000 = 29.8\,\mathrm{ms}$, the empirical p99 is $T_{(9900)} = 20\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the p99.9 is $T_{(9990)} =
1\,\mathrm{s}$. One user in a hundred waits fifty times longer than the median, which the mean barely shows.
:::

Dean and Barroso list where variability comes from. Queueing is one source among several.

::: {#exm-lat-dean-sources}
#### Sources of variability

Besides queueing, Dean and Barroso name shared resources, background daemons, global resource sharing, maintenance
activities, power limits, garbage collection and energy management [@dean2013tail, pp. 75-76]. Most of them make a
server briefly slower; queueing then turns a brief slowdown into a backlog that later requests also wait for, which is
what the queueing models of this chapter quantify.
:::

The tail of one server becomes the common case of a request that waits for many. The previous chapter proved how.

::: {#exm-lat-fan-out}
#### Fan-out

By the fan-out rule of @prp-fan-out-tail, a request that waits for $100$ servers, each slower than $1\,\mathrm{s}$ with
probability $0.01$, is slower than $1\,\mathrm{s}$ with probability $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$, the "63%" of
@dean2013tail [p. 76]. The p99 of one server is the median of the request. The rule is not proved again here; it is used
whenever a request fans out.
:::

MapReduce met the same effect in batch jobs. A few slow tasks set the completion time of the whole job.

::: {#exm-lat-stragglers}
#### Stragglers

A common cause of slow MapReduce jobs is "a 'straggler': a machine that takes an unusually long time to complete one of
the last few map or reduce tasks"; with backup executions of the last tasks, a sort "takes 44% longer to complete when
the backup task mechanism is disabled", while the backups cost "no more than a few percent" of resources
[@dean2004mapreduce, Sec. 3.6]. A job is a fan-out over its tasks, and its response time is that of the slowest.
:::

Utilisation is an average over servers. Zukerman's example has two.

::: {#exm-lat-utilisation}
#### Utilisation of two servers

"If you have two identical servers and one is busy 0.4 of the time and the other 0.6. Then, the utilization is 0.5"
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.2, p. 107]. By item 3 the pool's utilisation is $(0.4 + 0.6)/2$; the busier server's
requests may still wait much longer than the other's.
:::

Gilbert's RED method monitors three of the quantities of the definition. Each has its item.

::: {#exm-lat-red}
#### Rate, errors, duration

The RED method "recommends monitoring rate, error, and duration metrics for each service": "Rate – The number of
successful requests/events per unit of time", "Errors – The rate of failed requests/events", "Duration – The amount of time
(that is, latency) needed to process requests/events" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 12, "The RED
method"]. Rate is the throughput of item 1 and duration is the distribution of item 2, reported by its percentiles.
:::

Libraries offer several definitions of a sample quantile. Item 2 is the one that returns a measured value.

::: {#exm-lat-empirical-quantile}
#### Computing the empirical quantile

For $n = 1000$ seeded response times, $T_{(\lceil 0.99 n\rceil)} = T_{(990)}$ is NumPy's quantile with the method
`inverted_cdf`; NumPy's default interpolates between neighbouring order statistics and returns a value that was never
measured.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(20), sigma=0.6, size=1000)     # response times in ms
by_definition = np.sort(t)[int(np.ceil(0.99 * len(t))) - 1]
print(f"T_(990) = {by_definition:.2f} ms; inverted_cdf {np.quantile(t, 0.99, method='inverted_cdf'):.2f} ms; "
      f"default (linear) {np.quantile(t, 0.99):.2f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
T_(990) = 73.92 ms; inverted_cdf 73.92 ms; default (linear) 73.93 ms
```
:::

Sinha and Chopra list what latency depends on. One item on their list is the subject of this chapter.

::: {#exm-lat-sinha-factors}
#### What latency depends on

"Latency can be influenced by a variety of factors, including the distance between nodes in the system, network
congestion, processing time at each node, and the size and complexity of the data being transmitted"
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 2, "Latency"]. Distance and size were the subject of the previous chapters; congestion,
in a server as in a network, is waiting for a busy resource, which the queueing models of the following sections
predict from the load.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the summaries of item 2 for a sample. It uses the order-statistic definition.

::: {#exr-lat-percentiles}
#### Percentiles of a sample

For $10^5$ seeded response times, lognormal with median $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ and shape $\sigma = 0.8$, give the mean, the
median and the p99 and p99.9 by item 2. By what factor is the p99.9 above the median?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For a lognormal law with median $m$ and shape $\sigma$ the $q$-quantile is $me^{\sigma z_q}$, with $z_{0.99} = 2.33$ and
$z_{0.999} = 3.09$, so the p99 is about $129\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the p99.9 about $236\,\mathrm{ms}$, twelve times the
median; the mean is $me^{\sigma^2/2} = 27.5\,\mathrm{ms}$. The sample's values agree to within the sampling error.

## Python

The sample's summaries.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
t = np.sort(rng.lognormal(np.log(20), 0.8, 100_000))
q = lambda p: t[int(np.ceil(p * len(t))) - 1]
print(f"mean {t.mean():.1f}, median {q(0.5):.1f}, p99 {q(0.99):.1f}, p99.9 {q(0.999):.1f} ms; "
      f"p99.9 / median = {q(0.999) / q(0.5):.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean 27.5, median 20.0, p99 128.3, p99.9 231.7 ms; p99.9 / median = 11.6
```
::::
:::

The second exercise shows a common error in dashboards. Percentiles of parts cannot be averaged into the percentile of the
whole.

::: {#exr-lat-merge-percentiles}
#### Averaging percentiles

Server A answers $9000$ requests in $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ each and server B $1000$ requests, half in $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ and half
in $500\,\mathrm{ms}$. Give each server's p99, their average, and the p99 of all $10\,000$ requests. What must a monitoring
system keep to report the true p99 of a fleet?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A's p99 is $10\,\mathrm{ms}$; B's is $500\,\mathrm{ms}$ ($500$ of its $1000$ are slow); the average is $255\,\mathrm{ms}$. Of
all requests, $500$ in $10\,000$, $5\%$, are slow, so the p99 is $500\,\mathrm{ms}$: the average understates it by half.
A fleet's percentile needs the merged samples, or histograms with common buckets that can be added, not the servers'
percentiles.

## Python

The three numbers.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
a = np.full(9000, 10.0)
b = np.concatenate([np.full(500, 10.0), np.full(500, 500.0)])
p99 = lambda t: np.sort(t)[int(np.ceil(0.99 * len(t))) - 1]
print(f"A {p99(a)}, B {p99(b)}, average {(p99(a) + p99(b)) / 2}, merged {p99(np.concatenate([a, b]))} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A 10.0, B 500.0, average 255.0, merged 500.0 ms
```
::::
:::

The third exercise separates throughput from the arrival rate. An overloaded server completes only its capacity.

::: {#exr-lat-overload}
#### Throughput under overload

A server of capacity $\mu = 2000$ requests per second, each taking exactly $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$, receives $2500$ requests per
second, evenly spaced, for $10\,\mathrm{s}$. Give its throughput, the number of requests waiting at the end, and the
response time of the last request to arrive. What happens to the response time as the window grows?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The server is never idle after the first request, so it completes $2000$ per second: $X = 2000$ while the arrival rate is
$2500$. After $10\,\mathrm{s}$, $25\,000$ have arrived and $20\,000$ have completed, so about $5000$ wait. The last arrival
waits for those ahead of it, $5000 \times 0.5\,\mathrm{ms} = 2.5\,\mathrm{s}$. The response time grows linearly with the
window: an overloaded system has no steady state.

## Python

The completion times of evenly spaced requests at a single server.

```{.python .run}
lam, service, seconds = 2500, 0.0005, 10
arrivals = [i / lam for i in range(lam * seconds)]
done, free = [], 0.0
for a in arrivals:
    free = max(free, a) + service
    done.append(free)
completed = sum(d <= seconds for d in done)
print(f"throughput {completed / seconds:.0f}/s; waiting at the end {len(arrivals) - completed}; "
      f"last response time {done[-1] - arrivals[-1]:.3f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
throughput 2000/s; waiting at the end 5001; last response time 2.500 s
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise computes utilisation from a server's log of busy periods. It is item 3 applied to data.

::: {#exr-lat-busy-periods}
#### Utilisation from a log

A server was busy during $[0, 0.4]$, $[1.0, 1.7]$, $[2.0, 2.2]$ and $[3.5, 4.6]$ seconds of a $5$-second window, and completed
$9$ requests. Give its utilisation, its throughput and the mean service time per request. Which relation between them holds?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Busy time $0.4 + 0.7 + 0.2 + 1.1 = 2.4\,\mathrm{s}$, utilisation $2.4/5 = 0.48$, throughput $9/5 = 1.8$ per second, mean
service time $2.4/9 = 0.267\,\mathrm{s}$. Utilisation is throughput times mean service time, $1.8 \times 0.267 = 0.48$,
because both sides are the busy time divided by the window.

## Python

The three quantities and the identity.

```{.python .run}
busy = [(0, 0.4), (1.0, 1.7), (2.0, 2.2), (3.5, 4.6)]
window, completed = 5.0, 9
b = sum(e - s for s, e in busy)
U, X, S = b / window, completed / window, b / completed
print(f"utilisation {U:.3f}, throughput {X:.2f}/s, mean service {S:.4f} s, X * S = {X * S:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
utilisation 0.480, throughput 1.80/s, mean service 0.2667 s, X * S = 0.480
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise computes the p99 of a two-part distribution. A cache in front of a database produces one.

::: {#exr-lat-hit-miss}
#### Hits and misses

$90\%$ of requests hit a cache and take $5\,\mathrm{ms}$; the others miss and take $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ plus an exponentially
distributed database time of mean $40\,\mathrm{ms}$. Compute the p99 exactly and the mean. What if the hit ratio rises to
$99.5\%$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The p99 is a time $t > 5$ with $\mathbb P(T > t) = 0.1e^{-(t - 5)/40} = 0.01$, so $t = 5 + 40\log 10 = 97.1\,\mathrm{ms}$;
the mean is $5 + 0.1 \times 40 = 9\,\mathrm{ms}$. With $99.5\%$ hits, $\mathbb P(T > 5) = 0.005 < 0.01$, so the p99 is
$5\,\mathrm{ms}$: the tail moved past the percentile, while the mean only fell to $5.2\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The exact quantile and a seeded check.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import log
for hit in (0.9, 0.995):
    miss = 1 - hit
    exact = 5 + 40 * log(miss / 0.01) if miss > 0.01 else 5.0
    rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
    t = 5 + np.where(rng.random(200_000) < miss, rng.exponential(40, 200_000), 0.0)
    print(f"hit ratio {hit}: p99 {exact:.1f} ms (sample {np.quantile(t, 0.99, method='inverted_cdf'):.1f}), "
          f"mean {5 + miss * 40:.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
hit ratio 0.9: p99 97.1 ms (sample 97.1), mean 9.0 ms
hit ratio 0.995: p99 5.0 ms (sample 5.0), mean 5.2 ms
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise uses part (b) of the fan-out rule. A request's percentile is a higher percentile of each call.

::: {#exr-lat-fan-out-quantile}
#### The percentile a shard must meet

A search waits for $50$ shards with independent exponential response times of mean $10\,\mathrm{ms}$. Using part (b) of
@prp-fan-out-tail, give the request's p99, and the mean a shard would need for the request's p99 to be $50\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The request's p99 is the shard's $0.99^{1/50} = 0.999799$-quantile, $-10\log(1 - 0.999799) = 85.1\,\mathrm{ms}$, for a
shard whose own p99 is $46\,\mathrm{ms}$. For $50\,\mathrm{ms}$ the mean must be $50/8.51 = 5.9\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The quantile of the maximum, and a seeded check.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import log
n, mean = 50, 10.0
level = 0.99 ** (1 / n)
p99 = -mean * log(1 - level)
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
sim = rng.exponential(mean, size=(100_000, n)).max(axis=1)
print(f"shard level {level:.6f}; request p99 {p99:.1f} ms (simulated {np.quantile(sim, 0.99):.1f}); "
      f"mean needed for 50 ms: {50 / -log(1 - level):.2f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
shard level 0.999799; request p99 85.1 ms (simulated 84.8); mean needed for 50 ms: 5.87 ms
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise bounds the error of a percentile read from a histogram. Monitoring systems store counts in
buckets, not every sample.

::: {#exr-lat-histogram}
#### Percentiles from buckets

Response times are counted in buckets $[b_j, b_{j+1})$ with $b_{j+1} = 1.1\,b_j$, and the p99 is reported as the upper
bound $b_{j+1}$ of the bucket that contains $\hat t_{0.99}$. Prove that the report lies within $10\%$ above the empirical
p99, and check it on a seeded sample.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\hat t_{0.99} \in [b_j, b_{j+1})$, the report is $b_{j+1} = 1.1\,b_j \leq 1.1\,\hat t_{0.99}$, and $b_{j+1} >
\hat t_{0.99}$; so $\hat t_{0.99} < \text{report} \leq 1.1\,\hat t_{0.99}$. The bucket containing $\hat t_{0.99}$ is found from
the counts alone: it is the first bucket whose cumulative count reaches $\lceil 0.99n\rceil$. A factor of $1.1$ between
buckets covers $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ to $10\,\mathrm{s}$ with $97$ buckets.

## Python

The bucketed report and the exact value.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import ceil, log
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
t = rng.lognormal(np.log(20), 0.8, 50_000)
edges = 1.0 * 1.1 ** np.arange(0, 100)
counts, _ = np.histogram(t, bins=edges)
k = int(np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(counts), ceil(0.99 * len(t))))
exact = np.sort(t)[ceil(0.99 * len(t)) - 1]
print(f"exact p99 {exact:.2f} ms, bucket report {edges[k + 1]:.2f} ms, ratio {edges[k + 1] / exact:.3f}; "
      f"buckets for 1 ms..10 s: {ceil(log(1e4) / log(1.1))}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
exact p99 129.12 ms, bucket report 142.04 ms, ratio 1.100; buckets for 1 ms..10 s: 97
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise checks a latency requirement window by window. A requirement on a percentile is a statement about
each window, not about a day.

::: {#exr-lat-slo-windows}
#### A requirement per minute

The feed's requirement is $t_{0.99} \leq 500\,\mathrm{ms}$ in every minute. In a seeded hour of $60$ minutes of $6000$
requests each, responses are lognormal with median $80\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $\sigma = 0.7$, except during a five-minute
incident in which $\sigma = 1.2$. Count the minutes that violate the requirement, and compare with the p99 of the whole
hour.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

In normal minutes the p99 is about $80e^{0.7 \times 2.33} = 408\,\mathrm{ms}$; during the incident about $80e^{1.2 \times
2.33} = 1310\,\mathrm{ms}$. The five incident minutes violate the requirement. The p99 of the whole hour mixes them with
the rest and stays below $500\,\mathrm{ms}$: a daily or hourly percentile can hide an incident that a per-minute one
reveals.

## Python

Per-minute and hourly percentiles.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
minutes = [rng.lognormal(np.log(80), 1.2 if 30 <= m < 35 else 0.7, 6000) for m in range(60)]
p99 = lambda t: np.quantile(t, 0.99, method="inverted_cdf")
bad = [m for m, t in enumerate(minutes) if p99(t) > 500]
print(f"violating minutes {bad}; hourly p99 {p99(np.concatenate(minutes)):.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
violating minutes [30, 31, 32, 33, 34]; hourly p99 490 ms
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise reads a capacity from a load test. Throughput follows the offered rate until it stops.

::: {#exr-lat-capacity}
#### Reading the capacity

A load test offers $500, 1000, \dots, 3000$ requests per second to one server and measures throughputs $500, 1000, 1500,
1980, 2010, 1990$. Estimate the capacity, and say what the response times must have done at the last three points.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Throughput equals the offered rate up to $1500$ and then stays near $2000$: the capacity is about $2000$ requests per second.
At the last three points the offered rate exceeds the capacity, so, as in @exr-lat-overload, a backlog grows during each
step and the response times grow with the step's length; requests may also time out, which the throughput hides.

## Python

The plateau.

```{.python .run}
offered = [500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000]
measured = [500, 1000, 1500, 1980, 2010, 1990]
for o, x in zip(offered, measured):
    print(f"offered {o:4d}: throughput {x:4d} ({'saturated' if x < 0.95 * o else 'keeps up'})")
print("capacity estimate:", round(sum(x for o, x in zip(offered, measured) if x < 0.95 * o) / 2), "per second")
```

```{.text .run-output}
offered  500: throughput  500 (keeps up)
offered 1000: throughput 1000 (keeps up)
offered 1500: throughput 1500 (keeps up)
offered 2000: throughput 1980 (keeps up)
offered 2500: throughput 2010 (saturated)
offered 3000: throughput 1990 (saturated)
capacity estimate: 2000 per second
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise quantifies backup tasks. A backup issued late costs little and removes most of the tail.

::: {#exr-lat-backup}
#### Backups for the last tasks

A job has $200$ tasks; each takes $1$ unit of time, except that with probability $0.02$ a task's machine is a straggler
and the task takes $20$. A backup copy of every task still running at time $1.5$ is started on a healthy machine. Simulate
the job's completion time with and without backups, and the extra work.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Without backups the job almost always waits for a straggler: with $200$ tasks, $1 - 0.98^{200} = 0.98$ of jobs contain one,
and those take $20$. With backups a straggling task finishes at $1.5 + 1 = 2.5$ (the backup is healthy, and with probability
$0.02$ a straggler too, and then the task still takes $20$). The mean completion time falls from about $19.7$ to about $3.8$,
the rest coming from the rare jobs whose backup also straggles, and the extra work is about $5$ task-units, under $3\%$ of the
job, which is Dean and Ghemawat's "no more than a few percent".

## Python

A seeded simulation of $2000$ jobs.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
jobs, tasks = 2000, 200
slow = rng.random((jobs, tasks)) < 0.02
time = np.where(slow, 20.0, 1.0)
backup_slow = rng.random((jobs, tasks)) < 0.02
with_backup = np.where(time > 1.5, np.minimum(time, 1.5 + np.where(backup_slow, 20.0, 1.0)), time)
extra = np.where(time > 1.5, np.minimum(time, 1.5 + np.where(backup_slow, 20.0, 1.0)) - 1.5, 0).sum(axis=1)
print(f"mean completion without backups {time.max(axis=1).mean():.2f}, with {with_backup.max(axis=1).mean():.2f}; "
      f"extra work {extra.mean():.1f} task-units ({extra.mean() / tasks:.1%})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean completion without backups 19.69, with 3.78; extra work 5.3 task-units (2.7%)
```
::::
:::
::::

### How many samples a percentile needs

A load test that records $100$ requests cannot report a p99.9, and one that records $300$ barely sees the p99. How many
measurements are needed, and how far from the true percentile the empirical one may lie, follows from one observation:
the number of measurements below the true percentile is binomial. The proposition turns it into exact confidence
intervals that hold whatever the distribution of the response time, provided it has no atoms. It uses the binomial
distribution of
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-quantile-estimate}
#### Order statistics and quantiles

Let $T_1, \dots, T_n$ be independent with a common continuous distribution function $F$, let $q \in (0, 1)$ and $t_q$ be a
$q$-quantile, so that $F(t_q) = q$, let $T_{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq T_{(n)}$ be the order statistics, and let $B \sim
\operatorname{Bin}(n, q)$.

(a) For $1 \leq j \leq n$, $\mathbb P(T_{(j)} \leq t_q) = \mathbb P(B \geq j)$.

(b) For $1 \leq j < k \leq n$, $\mathbb P(T_{(j)} \leq t_q < T_{(k)}) = \mathbb P(j \leq B \leq k - 1)$: the interval
$[T_{(j)}, T_{(k)})$ contains $t_q$ with this probability, whatever $F$ is.

(c) $\mathbb P(T_{(n)} \leq t_q) = q^n$: at least one measurement exceeds $t_q$ with probability $1 - q^n$, which is at least
$1 - \alpha$ if and only if $n \geq \log\alpha/\log q$.

(d) The number of measurements above $t_q$ is $\operatorname{Bin}(n, 1 - q)$, with mean $n(1 - q)$ and variance $nq(1 - q)$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* Let $B = \sum_i\mathbf 1\{T_i \leq t_q\}$. The indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter
$\mathbb P(T_i \leq t_q) = F(t_q) = q$, so $B \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, q)$ by the trials property of the
[binomial distribution](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution).

(a) $T_{(j)} \leq t_q$ holds exactly when at least $j$ of the measurements are at most $t_q$, that is when $B \geq j$.

(b) Since $T_{(j)} \leq T_{(k)}$, the event $\{T_{(k)} \leq t_q\}$ is contained in $\{T_{(j)} \leq t_q\}$, and the
difference is $\{T_{(j)} \leq t_q < T_{(k)}\}$. By (a) its probability is $\mathbb P(B \geq j) - \mathbb P(B \geq k) =
\mathbb P(j \leq B \leq k - 1)$.

(c) By (a) with $j = n$, $\mathbb P(T_{(n)} \leq t_q) = \mathbb P(B = n) = q^n$. Then $1 - q^n \geq 1 - \alpha$ means $q^n
\leq \alpha$, that is $n\log q \leq \log\alpha$, and dividing by $\log q < 0$ reverses the inequality.

(d) The number above $t_q$ is $n - B$, the number of failures in $n$ trials with success probability $q$, which is
$\operatorname{Bin}(n, 1 - q)$ with the binomial mean and variance. $\square$

The proposition is free of assumptions about $F$ beyond continuity, which is why the intervals are called
distribution-free. It also shows what a single empirical percentile is worth: by (a) with $j = \lceil qn\rceil$, the
probability that $\hat t_q$ falls below the true quantile is $\mathbb P(B \geq \lceil qn\rceil)$, close to one half for
large $n$, so an empirical p99 is as likely to be too low as too high, and its spread is that of $B$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first use of part (b) is an interval for a p99 from a thousand measurements. The indices come from the binomial
distribution.

::: {#exm-qest-ci-1000}
#### An interval for a p99

For $n = 1000$ and $q = 0.99$, the run below finds $j$ and $k$ around $\lceil qn\rceil = 990$ with $\mathbb P(j \leq B \leq
k - 1) \geq 0.95$. The interval $[T_{(j)}, T_{(k)})$ then contains the true p99 with at least that probability. Its
upper end is close to the sample's largest values: a thousand measurements locate the p99 only roughly.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
n, q = 1000, 0.99
pmf = [comb(n, i) * q**i * (1 - q)**(n - i) for i in range(n + 1)]
best = None
for j in range(970, 991):
    for k in range(991, n + 1):
        cover = sum(pmf[j:k])
        if cover >= 0.95 and (best is None or k - j < best[1] - best[0]):
            best = (j, k, cover)
print(f"j = {best[0]}, k = {best[1]}, coverage {best[2]:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
j = 983, k = 996, coverage 0.9575
```
:::

Part (c) answers the simplest question: how many measurements before one of them is above the p99. The answer is about
three hundred.

::: {#exm-qest-299}
#### Seeing the p99 at all

For $\alpha = 0.05$ and $q = 0.99$, part (c) needs $n \geq \log 0.05/\log 0.99 = 298.1$, that is $n \geq 299$. With fewer
measurements, a test may well report a largest value below the true p99, and no percentile it reports says anything about
the p99.
:::

The p99.9 needs ten times more. The same formula applies.

::: {#exm-qest-p999}
#### Seeing the p99.9

For $q = 0.999$ part (c) gives $n \geq \log 0.05/\log 0.999 = 2994.2$, so $2995$ measurements. Tan's consumer apps with
targets of "tens of milliseconds to several seconds" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.4, p. 65] need thousands of
requests per test point before their high percentiles are worth reporting.
:::

Part (d) says how many measurements sit in the tail. They are few, and their number fluctuates.

::: {#exm-qest-tail-count}
#### How many are in the tail

Of $10^4$ measurements, $\operatorname{Bin}(10^4, 0.01)$ lie above the true p99: $100$ on average with standard deviation
$\sqrt{10^4 \times 0.99 \times 0.01} = 9.95$. The empirical p99 is determined by these hundred values, and their count
varies by about $10\%$ from test to test.
:::

A load test is limited by its duration. A minute at $100$ requests per second gives $6000$ measurements.

::: {#exm-qest-minute}
#### One minute of load

With $n = 6000$, $\lceil 0.99n\rceil = 5940$, and $B$ has mean $5940$ and standard deviation $7.7$. By the normal
approximation of the binomial, part (b) with $j = 5925$ and $k = 5956$ gives coverage about $95\%$: the p99 lies between the
$76$th and the $45$th largest measurements, a ratio that depends on the shape of the tail.
:::

The coverage of part (b) holds whatever $F$ is. A seeded simulation with a heavy-tailed law checks it.

::: {#exm-qest-coverage}
#### Checking the coverage

With $n = 1000$, $j = 980$ and $k = 997$, part (b) predicts the coverage $\mathbb P(980 \leq B \leq 996)$ for every
continuous law; $20\,000$ seeded samples from a Pareto law with exponent $1.5$ give the same fraction.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import comb
n, q, j, k = 1000, 0.99, 980, 997
predicted = sum(comb(n, i) * q**i * (1 - q)**(n - i) for i in range(j, k))
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
t99 = 100 ** (1 / 1.5)                                     # Pareto(1.5) on [1, oo): P(T > t) = t^-1.5
samples = np.sort(rng.pareto(1.5, size=(20_000, n)) + 1, axis=1)
covered = np.mean((samples[:, j - 1] <= t99) & (t99 < samples[:, k - 1]))
print(f"predicted coverage {predicted:.4f}, simulated {covered:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
predicted coverage 0.9884, simulated 0.9880
```
:::

A requirement can be tested with part (a). The question is whether the measurements are compatible with it.

::: {#exm-qest-requirement-test}
#### Testing a requirement

The feed must have $t_{0.99} \leq 500\,\mathrm{ms}$. In $n = 1000$ measurements, $18$ exceed $500\,\mathrm{ms}$. If the
requirement held with equality, the number above would be $\operatorname{Bin}(1000, 0.01)$ by part (d), and $18$ or more
would occur with probability $0.014$ (and with less if the true p99 were lower): strong evidence that the requirement is
violated.
:::

Zukerman's confidence intervals are for means. They do not carry over to percentiles directly.

::: {#exm-qest-zukerman-means}
#### Means and percentiles

Zukerman's interval for a simulated mean is $\bar a \pm t\,\sigma_a/\sqrt n$, using Student's $t$ distribution with $n - 1$
degrees of freedom [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 4.1, p. 118]. It concerns an average of independent observations; a
percentile is not an average, and its uncertainty is that of a binomial count, as part (b) shows. Both need independent
observations, which the response times of consecutive requests to one server often are not.
:::

Reporting the largest of a few values as a p99 is a common error. Part (c) shows how often it is wrong.

::: {#exm-qest-max-not-p99}
#### The maximum of fifty

A test with $50$ requests reports its largest response time as the p99. By part (c) the largest is below the true p99 with
probability $0.99^{50} = 0.61$: more often than not, the report is an underestimate.
:::

For large $n$ the indices of part (b) follow from the normal approximation. The rule is $nq \pm z\sqrt{nq(1 - q)}$.

::: {#exm-qest-normal-indices}
#### Indices by the normal approximation

With $z = 1.96$, $n = 10^5$ and $q = 0.99$, $nq = 99\,000$ and $\sqrt{nq(1 - q)} = 31.5$, so $j = 98\,939$ and $k = 99\,062$
give about $95\%$; the exact binomial sum, computed below, agrees.

```{.python .run}
from math import lgamma, log, exp, sqrt, floor, ceil
n, q, z = 10**5, 0.99, 1.96
sd = sqrt(n * q * (1 - q))
j, k = floor(n * q - z * sd), ceil(n * q + z * sd) + 1
logpmf = lambda i: lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(i + 1) - lgamma(n - i + 1) + i * log(q) + (n - i) * log(1 - q)
print(f"j = {j}, k = {k}, exact coverage {sum(exp(logpmf(i)) for i in range(j, k)):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
j = 98938, k = 99063, exact coverage 0.9530
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes an interval for the p95 from five hundred measurements. It applies part (b) directly.

::: {#exr-qest-p95}
#### An interval for a p95

For $n = 500$ and $q = 0.95$, find the shortest pair $j < k$ with $\mathbb P(j \leq B \leq k - 1) \geq 0.95$, and give its
coverage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$B \sim \operatorname{Bin}(500, 0.95)$ has mean $475$ and standard deviation $4.9$, so the pair lies about ten indices on
either side of $475$; the search below finds the shortest pair and its exact coverage.

## Python

The search over pairs.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
n, q = 500, 0.95
pmf = [comb(n, i) * q**i * (1 - q)**(n - i) for i in range(n + 1)]
best = min(((j, k) for j in range(455, 476) for k in range(476, 497) if sum(pmf[j:k]) >= 0.95), key=lambda p: p[1] - p[0])
print(f"j = {best[0]}, k = {best[1]}, coverage {sum(pmf[best[0]:best[1]]):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
j = 464, k = 484, coverage 0.9533
```
::::
:::

The second exercise is the median case. The interval is then symmetric.

::: {#exr-qest-median}
#### An interval for the median

Prove that for the median ($q = 1/2$) and $1 \leq j \leq n/2$, $\mathbb P(T_{(j)} \leq t_{0.5} < T_{(n + 1 - j)}) = 1 -
2\,\mathbb P(B \leq j - 1)$, and give the $j$ for $n = 100$ that gives at least $95\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (b) with $k = n + 1 - j$ the probability is $\mathbb P(j \leq B \leq n - j) = 1 - \mathbb P(B \leq j - 1) -
\mathbb P(B \geq n + 1 - j)$. For $q = 1/2$ the law of $B$ is symmetric, $\mathbb P(B = i) = \mathbb P(B = n - i)$, so
$\mathbb P(B \geq n + 1 - j) = \mathbb P(B \leq j - 1)$. For $n = 100$ the largest $j$ with $\mathbb P(B \leq j - 1) \leq
0.025$ is $j = 40$, so $[T_{(40)}, T_{(61)})$ covers the median with at least $95\%$.

## Python

The largest $j$.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
n = 100
cdf = lambda m: sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(m + 1)) / 2**n
j = max(j for j in range(1, n // 2 + 1) if cdf(j - 1) <= 0.025)
print(f"j = {j}, interval [T_({j}), T_({n + 1 - j})), coverage {1 - 2 * cdf(j - 1):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
j = 40, interval [T_(40), T_(61)), coverage 0.9648
```
::::
:::

The third exercise finds the smallest sample that has a two-sided interval for the p99 at all. Part (b) needs $k \leq n$.

::: {#exr-qest-smallest-n}
#### When an upper end exists

An interval $[T_{(j)}, T_{(k)})$ with $k \leq n$ can cover the p99 with probability at least $0.95$ only if $\mathbb P(B \leq
n - 1) \geq 0.95$. Find the smallest such $n$, and explain the connection with part (c).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Even with $j = 1$ and $k = n$ the coverage is $\mathbb P(1 \leq B \leq n - 1) \leq \mathbb P(B \leq n - 1) = 1 - q^n$. This is
at least $0.95$ exactly when $n \geq 299$, the bound of part (c): below $299$ measurements no interval inside the sample
covers the p99 with $95\%$, because the sample's maximum is too often below it.

## Python

The smallest $n$.

```{.python .run}
n = 1
while 1 - 0.99**n < 0.95:
    n += 1
print("smallest n:", n, "| coverage bound", round(1 - 0.99**n, 4))
```

```{.text .run-output}
smallest n: 299 | coverage bound 0.9505
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise checks the coverage of the interval of @exm-qest-ci-1000 on a lognormal law. The proposition says the
law does not matter.

::: {#exr-qest-lognormal-coverage}
#### Coverage on another law

With the $j$ and $k$ found in @exm-qest-ci-1000, simulate $10\,000$ samples of $1000$ lognormal response times (median
$20\,\mathrm{ms}$, $\sigma = 0.6$), and give the fraction of intervals that contain the true p99, $20e^{0.6 z_{0.99}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The fraction is the binomial probability of part (b) up to sampling error, as for the Pareto law of @exm-qest-coverage: the
interval's coverage depends only on $n$, $q$, $j$ and $k$.

## Python

The simulation, recomputing $j$ and $k$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import comb, exp
n, q = 1000, 0.99
pmf = [comb(n, i) * q**i * (1 - q)**(n - i) for i in range(n + 1)]
j, k = min(((j, k) for j in range(970, 991) for k in range(991, n + 1) if sum(pmf[j:k]) >= 0.95), key=lambda p: p[1] - p[0])
true_p99 = 20 * exp(0.6 * 2.3263479)
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
s = np.sort(rng.lognormal(np.log(20), 0.6, size=(10_000, n)), axis=1)
print(f"j = {j}, k = {k}: predicted {sum(pmf[j:k]):.4f}, simulated {np.mean((s[:, j - 1] <= true_p99) & (true_p99 < s[:, k - 1])):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
j = 983, k = 996: predicted 0.9575, simulated 0.9569
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise computes the probability behind @exm-qest-requirement-test. It is a binomial tail.

::: {#exr-qest-test-pvalue}
#### How surprising are eighteen?

Prove that if the true p99 is at most $500\,\mathrm{ms}$, the number $Y$ of measurements above $500\,\mathrm{ms}$ satisfies
$\mathbb P(Y \geq m) \leq \mathbb P(Z \geq m)$ with $Z \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, 0.01)$, and compute it for $n = 1000$ and $m =
10, 14, 18$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $t_{0.99} \leq 500$, then $p = \mathbb P(T > 500) \leq \mathbb P(T > t_{0.99}) = 0.01$, and $Y \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n,
p)$. A binomial tail $\mathbb P(Y \geq m)$ is non-decreasing in $p$: couple the trials as $\mathbf 1\{U_i \leq p\}$ with
independent uniform $U_i$; raising $p$ can only turn failures into successes. So $\mathbb P(Y \geq m) \leq \mathbb P(Z \geq m)$.
The values are $0.54$, $0.13$ and $0.014$.

## Python

The three tails.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
n, p = 1000, 0.01
tail = lambda m: 1 - sum(comb(n, i) * p**i * (1 - p)**(n - i) for i in range(m))
for m in (10, 14, 18):
    print(f"P(Z >= {m}) = {tail(m):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(Z >= 10) = 0.5427
P(Z >= 14) = 0.1344
P(Z >= 18) = 0.0138
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise shows why the proposition needs a continuous law. Rounded measurements have atoms.

::: {#exr-qest-atoms}
#### Rounded measurements

Response times are recorded in whole milliseconds, with $\mathbb P(T \leq 96) = 0.97$ and $\mathbb P(T = 97) = 0.03$, so
that $t_{0.99} = 97\,\mathrm{ms}$. Show that part (a) fails for $n = 100$ and $j = 99$, by computing both sides.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Here $F(t_{0.99}) = F(97) = 1 \neq 0.99$, so $B = \#\{i : T_i \leq 97\}$ is $\operatorname{Bin}(100, 1)$ and $\mathbb
P(T_{(99)} \leq 97) = 1$, while $\mathbb P(\operatorname{Bin}(100, 0.99) \geq 99) = 0.736$. With atoms the probability in
part (a) is $\mathbb P(\operatorname{Bin}(n, F(t_q)) \geq j)$, and $F(t_q)$ may exceed $q$.

## Python

Both sides.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
n, j, q = 100, 99, 0.99
binom_tail = sum(comb(n, i) * q**i * (1 - q)**(n - i) for i in range(j, n + 1))
print(f"P(T_(99) <= t_0.99) = 1.0 for this law; P(Bin(100, 0.99) >= 99) = {binom_tail:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(T_(99) <= t_0.99) = 1.0 for this law; P(Bin(100, 0.99) >= 99) = 0.736
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise compares the number of tests needed until one shows a tail value. It is the geometric law.

::: {#exr-qest-waiting}
#### Waiting for a tail value

Prove that the number of requests until the first one above $t_q$ is geometric with parameter $1 - q$, with mean $1/(1 -
q)$, and that the probability that the first $n$ contain none is $q^n$, which is part (c).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The events $\{T_i > t_q\}$ are independent with probability $1 - F(t_q) = 1 - q$, so the index of the first success is
geometric with parameter $1 - q$ by the trials property of the
[geometric distribution](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution),
with mean $1/(1 - q)$; it exceeds $n$ when the first $n$ trials fail, with probability $q^n$. For the p99 the mean is $100$
requests, but the probability of none in $299$ is still $0.05$.

## Python

A seeded check of the mean.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
first = rng.geometric(0.01, 100_000)
print(f"mean {first.mean():.1f} (1/(1-q) = 100); P(first > 299) = {np.mean(first > 299):.4f} (0.99^299 = {0.99**299:.4f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean 100.0 (1/(1-q) = 100); P(first > 299) = 0.0497 (0.99^299 = 0.0495)
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise pools the measurements of several servers. The fleet's percentile needs the pooled sample.

::: {#exr-qest-pool}
#### Pooling for a fleet

Ten servers each record $500$ response times from the same law. Compare the interval of part (b) for the fleet's p99 from
the pooled $5000$ measurements with what one server's $500$ allow, using @exr-qest-smallest-n.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $500$ measurements an interval inside the sample exists (since $500 \geq 299$) but its upper index is close to $n$; with
$5000$ the indices are $\lceil qn\rceil = 4950$ give or take about $14$, a much narrower interval in rank. Pooling is allowed
when the servers' laws are the same; if one server is slower, the pooled p99 is the fleet's, which is what users see.

## Python

The shortest $95\%$ pairs for $n = 500$ and $n = 5000$, by the normal approximation for speed.

```{.python .run}
from math import sqrt, floor, ceil
for n in (500, 5000):
    sd = sqrt(n * 0.99 * 0.01)
    j, k = floor(0.99 * n - 1.96 * sd), min(n, ceil(0.99 * n + 1.96 * sd) + 1)
    print(f"n = {n}: j = {j}, k = {k} (k is {n - k} below the maximum)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 500: j = 490, k = 500 (k is 0 below the maximum)
n = 5000: j = 4936, k = 4965 (k is 35 below the maximum)
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise breaks the independence assumption. Repeated measurements make an interval too narrow.

::: {#exr-qest-dependence}
#### Correlated measurements

A load generator records each of $100$ independent response times ten times, as if they were $1000$ measurements. Compute
the coverage of the interval of @exm-qest-ci-1000 by simulation, and explain the result with part (b).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The thousand values are ten copies of a hundred, so the number below the true p99 is ten times a $\operatorname{Bin}(100,
0.99)$ count, not a $\operatorname{Bin}(1000, 0.99)$ one; its spread is $\sqrt{10}$ times larger, and the interval chosen for
$1000$ independent values covers far less often than $95\%$. Part (b) is exact only for independent measurements.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import comb
n, q = 1000, 0.99
pmf = [comb(n, i) * q**i * (1 - q)**(n - i) for i in range(n + 1)]
j, k = min(((j, k) for j in range(970, 991) for k in range(991, n + 1) if sum(pmf[j:k]) >= 0.95), key=lambda p: p[1] - p[0])
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
s = np.sort(np.repeat(rng.exponential(1.0, size=(10_000, 100)), 10, axis=1), axis=1)
true = np.log(100)
print(f"coverage with copies {np.mean((s[:, j - 1] <= true) & (true < s[:, k - 1])):.3f} (nominal {sum(pmf[j:k]):.3f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
coverage with copies 0.363 (nominal 0.957)
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise plans the length of a load test for a p99.9. It combines parts (b) and (c).

::: {#exr-qest-test-length}
#### How long to test

A test step runs at $200$ requests per second. How long must it last so that (a) one measurement above the true p99.9 is seen
with probability $0.95$, and (b) the standard deviation of the number above the p99.9 is at most $10\%$ of its mean?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) $n \geq 2995$ by part (c), $15\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) By part (d) the count has mean $0.001n$ and standard deviation
$\sqrt{0.000999n}$; the ratio is at most $0.1$ when $n \geq 0.999/(0.001 \times 0.01) = 99\,900$, about $8.3$ minutes. The
second criterion, a stable count in the tail, is the one that makes a reported p99.9 reproducible.

## Python

The two durations.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil, log
rate, q = 200, 0.999
n_a = ceil(log(0.05) / log(q))
n_b = ceil(q / ((1 - q) * 0.1**2))
print(f"(a) {n_a} requests, {n_a / rate:.1f} s; (b) {n_b} requests, {n_b / rate / 60:.1f} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(a) 2995 requests, 15.0 s; (b) 99900 requests, 8.3 min
```
::::
:::
::::

## Little's law {#sec-littles-law}

A system that receives $\lambda$ requests per second and keeps each for $W$ seconds holds, on average, $\lambda W$ of them
at once. Zukerman calls this "known as Little's formula" and notes that "its applicability is not limited to single-server
queues, or single-queue systems, or systems with infinite buffers" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, pp. 108-110]. The
law needs no assumption about the arrival process, the service times or the order of service, which is why it is the most
used result of the chapter: it converts a rate and a time into a number of requests in flight, threads, connections or
servers. Zukerman's derivation is graphical and assumes that the system empties infinitely often. This section states the
law for a single path of arrivals and departures, under assumptions that can be checked on a measured trace, and proves it
completely.

For more on this topic, see @zukerman2013introduction [Secs. 3.2-3.3 and Homework 3.3].

### The law

Let the system be anything with a boundary: a server, a pool, a queue without its servers, a whole data centre. Requests
cross the boundary inward and, later, outward. Three long-run averages describe it: the rate of arrivals, the mean time a
request spends inside, and the time-average number inside. The theorem says that if the first two exist, so does the
third, and it is their product.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-littles-law}
#### Little's law

Let requests $i = 1, 2, \dots$ enter a system at times $0 \leq a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots$ with $a_i \to \infty$, and let request
$i$ stay for a time $W_i \geq 0$, leaving at $d_i = a_i + W_i$. Let $A(t) = \#\{i : a_i \leq t\}$ be the number of arrivals by
time $t$ and $Q(t) = \#\{i : a_i \leq t < d_i\}$ the number in the system at time $t$. Suppose that the limits
$$
\lambda = \lim_{t \to \infty}\frac{A(t)}{t} \in (0, \infty) \qquad\text{and}\qquad W = \lim_{n \to \infty}\frac1n\sum_{i = 1}^nW_i
\in [0, \infty)
$$
exist. Then the time-average number in the system exists and
$$
L = \lim_{t \to \infty}\frac1t\int_0^tQ(s)\,ds = \lambda W .
$$
:::

::::

*Proof.* Each request contributes to $\int_0^tQ$ the length of the part of $[a_i, d_i)$ that lies in $[0, t]$, so
$$
\int_0^tQ(s)\,ds = \sum_{i \geq 1}\bigl|[a_i, d_i) \cap [0, t]\bigr| .
$$
*Upper bound.* Only requests with $a_i \leq t$ contribute, each at most $W_i$, so $\int_0^tQ \leq \sum_{i \leq A(t)}W_i$.
Dividing by $t$,
$$
\frac1t\int_0^tQ \leq \frac{A(t)}t\cdot\frac1{A(t)}\sum_{i \leq A(t)}W_i \to \lambda W,
$$
since $A(t) \to \infty$ (because $\lambda > 0$) and the averages converge to $W$.

*The stay of the $n$-th request is small compared with its arrival time.* Write $S_n = \sum_{i \leq n}W_i$. Then
$W_n/n = S_n/n - \frac{n - 1}n\cdot S_{n-1}/(n - 1) \to W - W = 0$. Next, $n/a_n \to \lambda$. The first $n$ requests
have arrived by $a_n$, so $A(a_n) \geq n$ and $n/a_n \leq A(a_n)/a_n \to \lambda$. Requests $n, n + 1, \dots$ arrive at or
after $a_n$, so $A(s) \leq n - 1$ for every $s < a_n$; with $s = a_n - 1$ (for $n$ large enough that $a_n > 1$),
$$
\frac{n - 1}{a_n} \geq \frac{A(a_n - 1)}{a_n - 1}\cdot\frac{a_n - 1}{a_n} \to \lambda .
$$
Hence $n/a_n \to \lambda$, and $W_n/a_n = (W_n/n)(n/a_n) \to 0$.

*Lower bound.* Fix $\epsilon > 0$. By the last step there is $n_0$ with $W_i \leq \epsilon a_i$ for all $i > n_0$. Let $t$ be
large enough that $d_i \leq t$ for every $i \leq n_0$. A request $i > n_0$ with $a_i \leq t/(1 + \epsilon)$ leaves at $d_i \leq
(1 + \epsilon)a_i \leq t$, so it contributes its whole $W_i$; so do the requests $i \leq n_0$. Hence
$$
\frac1t\int_0^tQ \geq \frac1t\sum_{i \leq A(t/(1 + \epsilon))}W_i = \frac{A(t/(1 + \epsilon))}{t}\cdot
\frac1{A(t/(1 + \epsilon))}\sum_{i \leq A(t/(1 + \epsilon))}W_i \to \frac{\lambda}{1 + \epsilon}W .
$$
So $\liminf_t\frac1t\int_0^tQ \geq \lambda W/(1 + \epsilon)$ for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $\limsup_t \leq \lambda W$; the limit
exists and equals $\lambda W$. $\square$

The hypotheses are about one path of the system and can be checked on a trace: arrivals at a stable rate and a finite
mean stay. Nothing is assumed about the distribution of arrivals or stays, the number of servers, the order of service or
independence. The second form of the law, $L_q = \lambda W_q$, is the theorem applied to the waiting room alone, with $W_i$
the time request $i$ waits before service [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, eq. (269)]. For a stationary random
system, the long-run averages of a typical path are its stationary means, which is how Zukerman writes the law,
$\mathbb E[Q] = \lambda\mathbb E[D]$ (*ibid.*, eq. (268)).

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Zukerman's amusement park pays the law out in dollars. Each visitor pays for the time spent inside.

::: {#exm-little-park}
#### The amusement park

If the park "charges every customer one dollar per unit of time spent in the park", it earns $\mathbb E[Q]$ dollars per unit
of time, one per visitor present; it also earns $\lambda$ visitors per unit time times $\mathbb E[D]$ dollars each, so
"$\lambda\mathbb E[D] = \mathbb E[Q]$" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, p. 109]. The proof of the theorem makes the
two ways of counting the income exact: the integral of $Q$ and the sum of the stays.
:::

The feed tier of the running example holds as many requests as its rate times its response time. The count sizes its
thread pools.

::: {#exm-little-feed}
#### Requests in flight in the feed tier

At the peak of $1.74 \times 10^5$ requests per second and a mean response time of $W = 50\,\mathrm{ms}$ inside the
application tier, $L = 1.74 \times 10^5 \times 0.05 = 8700$ requests are in progress at once, $60$ per server of $146$. A
server whose thread pool holds fewer than $60$ threads makes requests wait for a thread, which raises $W$ and therefore $L$.
:::

Applied to a single server's service position, the law gives the utilisation. Zukerman derives it this way.

::: {#exm-little-utilisation}
#### The utilisation law

Take as the system "just the server with space for at most one customer served at the server". Its mean stay is the mean
service time $1/\mu$ and its arrival rate is $\lambda$, and the number inside is $0$ or $1$, so its average is the fraction
of time busy: "$\hat U = \lambda/\mu$" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, p. 110]. A feed server at $1192$ requests per
second with $\mu = 2000$ is busy $60\%$ of the time, the $\rho_{\max}$ of @exm-load-servers.
:::

Tan relates throughput and latency by an inverse. Little's law shows what the relation really involves.

::: {#exm-little-tan-inverse}
#### Is throughput the inverse of latency?

Tan writes that "throughput/bandwidth is the inverse of latency. A system with low latency has high throughput"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Ch. 3, p. 55]. By the theorem $X = L/W$: throughput is the number in progress divided by the
latency. It is the inverse of latency only when one request is in progress at a time ($L = 1$); a pool with $8700$ requests in
flight and $W = 50\,\mathrm{ms}$ has a throughput of $1.74 \times 10^5$ per second, not $20$.
:::

A closed system always holds the same number of requests. Zukerman's homework solves one by the law alone.

::: {#exm-little-always-full}
#### A system that is always full

A system with $k$ servers always holds $N$ customers, a new one arriving whenever one leaves. Applying the law to the
servers gives $\lambda(1/\mu) = k$, so $\lambda = k\mu$; applying it to the whole system gives $\lambda\mathbb E[D] = N$, so
"$\mathbb E[D] = N/(k\mu)$" [@zukerman2013introduction, Homework 3.3, p. 115]. A load generator with $N$ virtual users and no
pauses is such a system.
:::

The law also sizes connection pools to a database. Each query holds a connection for its duration.

::: {#exm-little-connections}
#### A connection pool

The feed's servers send $3 \times 10^4$ queries per second to the database at the peak, each holding a connection for
$4\,\mathrm{ms}$. By the theorem, $120$ connections are in use on average across the tier, under one per server: a pool of
$5$ connections per server is ample, and one of $100$ per server would leave $14\,600$ idle connections open on the
database.
:::

Applied to the waiting room, the law relates the queue to the wait. Zukerman uses both forms.

::: {#exm-little-queue-form}
#### Waiting room and servers

The waiting room alone is a system whose requests stay $W_q$; the servers alone are one whose requests stay $1/\mu$. The
theorem gives $L_q = \lambda W_q$ and $L - L_q = \lambda/\mu$, so $L = L_q + \lambda/\mu$ and $W = W_q + 1/\mu$
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, eqs. (277)-(278)]: one law for each box, consistent with each other.
:::

The hypotheses fail for an overloaded system. The limit $W$ then does not exist.

::: {#exm-little-unstable}
#### When the law does not apply

The overloaded server of @exr-lat-overload receives $2500$ requests per second and completes $2000$. The $n$-th arrival, at
time $n/2500$, leaves at about $n/2000$, so $W_n \approx n/2000 - n/2500 = n/10\,000$, and the averages of the $W_i$ grow
without limit. The theorem's hypothesis fails, and so does its conclusion: $Q(t)$ grows like $500t$.
:::

The law holds on any single path, not only on average. A measured trace can be checked directly.

::: {#exm-little-trace}
#### Checking a trace

A seeded trace of a single server with irregular arrivals and service times, over $2 \times 10^5$ requests, gives the three
averages below; the time-average number agrees with the product of the other two to three digits, with no model of the
arrivals.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
n = 200_000
a = np.cumsum(rng.uniform(0, 1.0, n))                        # arrivals, mean gap 0.5
s = rng.gamma(2.0, 0.2, n)                                    # service times, mean 0.4
d = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    free = max(free, a[i]) + s[i]; d[i] = free
W, lam = np.mean(d - a), n / a[-1]
t_end = d.max()
area = np.sum(np.minimum(d, t_end) - a)                       # integral of Q over [0, t_end]
print(f"lambda {lam:.4f}, W {W:.4f}, lambda*W {lam * W:.4f}, time-average L {area / t_end:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda 2.0013, W 1.0379, lambda*W 2.0772, time-average L 2.0772
```
:::

Connections of a real-time service obey the law too. The stay is the session's length.

::: {#exm-little-websockets}
#### Open connections

If users open $10^4$ WebSocket sessions per second and keep each for $30$ minutes on average, the connection
servers hold $10^4 \times 1800 = 1.8 \times 10^7$ connections at once, which is how many connection servers of
[The web stack](../the-web-stack/index.qmd) the design needs. The rate of new sessions and their length are often easier to
estimate than the number connected.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the law in its three directions. Any two of $L$, $\lambda$ and $W$ give the third.

::: {#exr-little-three-ways}
#### Three directions

(a) A service holds $300$ requests on average and completes $6000$ per second; what is its mean response time? (b) A queue
has a mean wait of $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $40$ requests waiting on average; what is the arrival rate? (c) A cache handles
$5 \times 10^4$ lookups per second of $0.2\,\mathrm{ms}$ each; how many are in progress?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) $W = L/\lambda = 300/6000 = 50\,\mathrm{ms}$. (b) $\lambda = L_q/W_q = 40/0.02 = 2000$ per second. (c) $L = 5 \times 10^4 \times
0.0002 = 10$. In (a) the completion rate stands for $\lambda$, which is allowed in steady state because arrivals and
completions have the same long-run rate.

## Python

The three products and quotients.

```{.python .run}
print(f"(a) W = {300 / 6000 * 1000:.0f} ms; (b) lambda = {40 / 0.02:.0f}/s; (c) L = {5e4 * 0.0002:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(a) W = 50 ms; (b) lambda = 2000/s; (c) L = 10
```
::::
:::

The second exercise proves that arrivals and departures have the same rate under the hypotheses of the theorem. The
proof reuses a step of the theorem's.

::: {#exr-little-departure-rate}
#### Departures keep pace

Under the hypotheses of the theorem, prove that the number of departures by time $t$, $D(t) = \#\{i : d_i \leq t\}$,
satisfies $D(t)/t \to \lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$D(t) \leq A(t)$, since a request leaves after it arrives, so $\limsup D(t)/t \leq \lambda$. For the lower bound, fix
$\epsilon > 0$; as in the proof, for large $t$ every request with $a_i \leq t/(1 + \epsilon)$ has left by $t$, so $D(t) \geq
A(t/(1 + \epsilon))$ and $\liminf D(t)/t \geq \lambda/(1 + \epsilon)$. Since $\epsilon$ is arbitrary, $D(t)/t \to \lambda$:
a system satisfying the hypotheses has throughput equal to its arrival rate.

## Python

The two rates on the trace of @exm-little-trace, regenerated.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
n = 200_000
a = np.cumsum(rng.uniform(0, 1.0, n)); s = rng.gamma(2.0, 0.2, n)
d = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    free = max(free, a[i]) + s[i]; d[i] = free
t = a[-1] * 0.9
print(f"A(t)/t = {np.sum(a <= t) / t:.4f}, D(t)/t = {np.sum(d <= t) / t:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A(t)/t = 2.0007, D(t)/t = 2.0007
```
::::
:::

The third exercise evaluates Tan's inverse claim of @exm-little-tan-inverse numerically. Two systems with the same latency
can have very different throughputs.

::: {#exr-little-tan}
#### Same latency, different throughput

A single-threaded server and a server with $64$ threads both answer each request in $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ when kept busy. Give
their throughputs by the theorem, and the latency at which the $64$-thread server would have the single-threaded server's
throughput.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Kept busy, the first has $L = 1$ and $X = 1/0.01 = 100$ per second; the second has $L = 64$ and $X = 6400$ per second, with the
same latency. It would have $X = 100$ with $L = 64$ only if $W = 640\,\mathrm{ms}$. Throughput is concurrency divided by
latency, so the inverse holds only at a fixed concurrency of one.

## Python

The two throughputs.

```{.python .run}
for threads in (1, 64):
    print(f"{threads:2d} threads, W = 10 ms: X = {threads / 0.010:.0f}/s")
print(f"W giving X = 100 with 64 in flight: {64 / 100 * 1000:.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
 1 threads, W = 10 ms: X = 100/s
64 threads, W = 10 ms: X = 6400/s
W giving X = 100 with 64 in flight: 640 ms
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise sizes a thread pool from a latency budget. The law gives the number of threads needed.

::: {#exr-little-thread-pool}
#### Threads for a downstream call

Each feed request waits $W = 30\,\mathrm{ms}$ for a call to the ranking service, holding a thread meanwhile. A server receives
$1192$ requests per second. How many threads are busy with ranking calls on average, and what happens to the server if the
ranking service slows to $300\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the pool has $64$ threads?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$L = 1192 \times 0.03 = 35.8$ threads. At $300\,\mathrm{ms}$ the law would need $358$, more than the $64$ available: the pool is
exhausted, requests wait for threads, and the server's throughput falls to at most $64/0.3 = 213$ per second. A slow
dependency becomes a full pool; this is how one slow service brings down its callers.

## Python

The two cases.

```{.python .run}
rate, pool = 1192, 64
for w in (0.03, 0.3):
    need = rate * w
    print(f"W = {w * 1000:.0f} ms: threads needed {need:.1f}, pool {pool}, "
          f"max throughput {min(rate, pool / w):.0f}/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
W = 30 ms: threads needed 35.8, pool 64, max throughput 1192/s
W = 300 ms: threads needed 357.6, pool 64, max throughput 213/s
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise uses the law on two nested boxes. The difference of the two counts is the number in service.

::: {#exr-little-nested}
#### Two boxes

A service receives $800$ requests per second. Monitoring shows $L = 12$ requests in the system and $L_q = 4$ waiting. Give $W$,
$W_q$, the mean service time and the mean number of busy servers, using @exm-little-queue-form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$W = 12/800 = 15\,\mathrm{ms}$, $W_q = 4/800 = 5\,\mathrm{ms}$, so the mean service time is $10\,\mathrm{ms}$, and the mean number
of busy servers is $L - L_q = 8 = 800 \times 0.01$.

## Python

The four numbers.

```{.python .run}
lam, L, Lq = 800, 12, 4
W, Wq = L / lam, Lq / lam
print(f"W {W * 1000:.1f} ms, Wq {Wq * 1000:.1f} ms, service {(W - Wq) * 1000:.1f} ms, busy servers {L - Lq}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
W 15.0 ms, Wq 5.0 ms, service 10.0 ms, busy servers 8
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise uses the law to find the mean session length. Logs of logins are easier to count than sessions.

::: {#exr-little-session-length}
#### How long are sessions?

A chat service has $1.67 \times 10^7$ connected users at the peak (@exr-load-chat) and sees $4000$ new connections per second
then. Assuming the peak lasts long compared with a session, what is the mean connection length? What does the law require of
"long compared with a session"?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$W = L/\lambda = 1.67 \times 10^7/4000 = 4175\,\mathrm{s}$, about $70$ minutes. The theorem is a statement about long-run averages;
applied to a window, it is accurate when the window is long compared with the stays, so that requests in progress at its ends
are few compared with all requests in it. A peak hour is barely long enough for $70$-minute sessions.

## Python

The quotient.

```{.python .run}
print(f"mean connection {1.67e7 / 4000:.0f} s = {1.67e7 / 4000 / 60:.0f} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean connection 4175 s = 70 min
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise shows that the law needs a finite mean stay. A heavy-tailed stay breaks it.

::: {#exr-little-infinite-mean}
#### An infinite mean stay

Requests arrive at times $1, 2, 3, \dots$, and request $i$ stays $W_i = i^{1/2}$. Show that the hypothesis on $W$ fails, and
compute $\frac1t\int_0^tQ$ for growing $t$. Why does the conclusion fail too?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\frac1n\sum_{i \leq n}i^{1/2} \approx \frac23n^{1/2} \to \infty$, so $W$ does not exist. The number present at time $t$ is the number
of $i \leq t$ with $i + i^{1/2} > t$, about $t^{1/2}$, so the time average grows like $t^{1/2}$ too: there is no finite $L$.
Little's law is not violated; its hypothesis is.

## Python

The time averages for growing horizons.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
for t in (10**3, 10**4, 10**5):
    i = np.arange(1, t + 1)
    a, d = i.astype(float), i + np.sqrt(i)
    area = np.sum(np.clip(np.minimum(d, t) - a, 0, None))
    print(f"t = {t:>6}: average stay so far {np.mean(np.sqrt(i)):.1f}, time-average number {area / t:.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t =   1000: average stay so far 21.1, time-average number 20.6
t =  10000: average stay so far 66.7, time-average number 66.2
t = 100000: average stay so far 210.8, time-average number 210.3
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise derives the blocking probability from the law, as Zukerman does. A system that turns requests away
admits fewer than arrive.

::: {#exr-little-blocking}
#### Blocking from utilisation

A server with a finite buffer receives $\lambda = 1$ job per second with mean service time $0.8\,\mathrm{s}$, and is busy
$78.4\%$ of the time. Apply the law to the server alone to find the fraction of jobs blocked, as in
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, eq. (280), and Homework 3.5, p. 116].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The server's arrival rate is that of the admitted jobs, $(1 - P_b)\lambda$, its stay is $0.8\,\mathrm{s}$, and its mean
occupancy is the utilisation, so $0.784 = (1 - P_b) \times 1 \times 0.8$ and $P_b = 1 - 0.784/0.8 = 0.02$, Zukerman's $2\%$.

## Python

The blocking fraction.

```{.python .run}
U, lam, S = 0.784, 1.0, 0.8
print(f"P_b = {1 - U / (lam * S):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P_b = 0.020
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise bounds the error of the law on a finite window. The two sums of the proof differ only by requests at the
ends.

::: {#exr-little-window-error}
#### The law on a finite window

On a window $[0, t]$ that starts and ends with the system empty, prove that $\int_0^tQ(s)\,ds = \sum_{i \leq A(t)}W_i$ exactly,
so that $\frac1t\int_0^tQ = \frac{A(t)}t\cdot\frac1{A(t)}\sum_{i \leq A(t)}W_i$. Check it on a seeded trace cut at an empty
instant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If the system is empty at $t$, every request with $a_i \leq t$ has $d_i \leq t$, so its interval $[a_i, d_i)$ lies in $[0,
t]$ and contributes exactly $W_i$; requests with $a_i > t$ contribute nothing. The identity follows, and dividing by $t$
gives the law on the window with no error: this is Zukerman's argument, which assumes that the system empties
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.3, eq. (271)].

## Python

A trace cut at the last instant before $10^5$ at which the server is idle.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
n = 100_000
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1.0, n)); s = rng.exponential(0.7, n)
d = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    free = max(free, a[i]) + s[i]; d[i] = free
empty = [i for i in range(n - 1) if d[i] < a[i + 1] and a[i + 1] > 0.9 * a[-1]][0]   # idle between i and i + 1
t = d[empty]
events = sorted([(x, 1) for x in a[:empty + 1]] + [(x, -1) for x in d[:empty + 1]])
area, q, last = 0.0, 0, 0.0
for time, step in events:                                    # integrate Q(s) over [0, t] event by event
    area += q * (time - last); q += step; last = time
stays = np.sum(d[:empty + 1] - a[:empty + 1])
print(f"integral of Q {area:.3f}, sum of stays {stays:.3f}, "
      f"L {area / t:.4f}, lambda*W {(empty + 1) / t * stays / (empty + 1):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
integral of Q 213038.713, sum of stays 213038.713, L 2.3678, lambda*W 2.3678
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise sizes the feed's in-flight requests across the whole path. The law applies to each tier and to their
sum.

::: {#exr-little-path}
#### In flight along the path

A feed request spends $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ in the load balancer, $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ in the application server (of which
$5\,\mathrm{ms}$ in the cache and $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ in the database for the $30\%$ of requests that miss), at the peak rate of
$1.74 \times 10^5$ per second. Give the mean number of feed requests in each tier and in the whole service, and the mean
number at the database.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The balancer holds $1.74 \times 10^5 \times 0.005 = 870$, the application tier $6960$, the whole service $7830$, the sum. The
database receives $0.3 \times 1.74 \times 10^5 = 52\,200$ queries per second of $20\,\mathrm{ms}$, so it holds $1044$ at once.
Each count is the law for one box; the boxes' counts add because their stays do.

## Python

The counts.

```{.python .run}
lam = 1.74e5
lb, app = lam * 0.005, lam * 0.040
print(f"balancer {lb:.0f}, application {app:.0f}, service {lb + app:.0f}, database {0.3 * lam * 0.020:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
balancer 870, application 6960, service 7830, database 1044
```
::::
:::
::::

## Poisson arrivals and the M/M/1 queue {#sec-mm1}

Little's law relates averages but does not predict them: it cannot say how long requests wait at a server that is busy
$60\%$ of the time. A prediction needs a model of when requests arrive and how long they take. The simplest model that fits
many services is that arrivals come from many independent users, each rarely, which makes them a Poisson process, and that
service times are exponential. Zukerman describes the resulting single-server queue as "the simplest Markovian queue"
[@zukerman2013introduction, Ch. 6, p. 130]. This section defines the exponential distribution and the Poisson process and
proves the properties the queues use, then derives the M/M/1 queue: its queue-length distribution, its mean response time,
which grows without bound as the utilisation approaches one, and its percentiles.

For more on this topic, see @zukerman2013introduction [Secs. 2.2.2, 3.1, 3.8 and Ch. 6] and, for continuous-time Markov
chains and birth-death processes, [Random processes](../../complexity-science/random-processes/index.qmd#def-master-equation)
in Complexity Science.

### The Poisson process

A Poisson process can be defined in several equivalent ways. Zukerman gives three conditions (no arrival at time zero,
independent increments, Poisson counts) and notes that "a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ is a point process where the
inter-arrival times are independent and exponentially distributed random variables with mean $1/\lambda$"
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 2.2.2, pp. 77-78]. The definition below uses the second form, which is also how the
simulations of this chapter generate arrivals, and the properties after it are proved from it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-poisson-process}
#### Exponential distribution and Poisson process

A random variable $Y$ has the **exponential distribution** with rate $\lambda > 0$, $Y \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$, if
$\mathbb P(Y > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t \geq 0$; its density is $\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ and its mean $1/\lambda$. A
**Poisson process** of rate $\lambda$ is the sequence of arrival times $a_n = Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n$, $n \geq 1$, with $Y_1, Y_2,
\dots$ independent and $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$, together with its counting process $N(t) = \#\{n : a_n \leq t\}$. Then:

1. (**no memory**) $\mathbb P(Y > s + t \mid Y > s) = \mathbb P(Y > t)$ for $s, t \geq 0$;
2. (**competition**) if $Y_1', \dots, Y_k'$ are independent with $Y_j' \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_j)$ and $\Lambda =
   \lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_k$, then $\min_jY_j' \sim \operatorname{Exp}(\Lambda)$, and the minimum is $Y_j'$ with
   probability $\lambda_j/\Lambda$;
3. (**arrival times**) $a_n$ has the density $f_n(t) = \lambda^nt^{n-1}e^{-\lambda t}/(n - 1)!$ on $t > 0$, the Erlang
   distribution;
4. (**counts**) $N(t) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ for every $t > 0$;
5. (**rate**) $N(t)/t \to \lambda$ with probability one.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (1) $\mathbb P(Y > s + t \mid Y > s) = e^{-\lambda(s + t)}/e^{-\lambda s} = e^{-\lambda t}$.

(2) By independence $\mathbb P(\min_jY_j' > t) = \prod_je^{-\lambda_jt} = e^{-\Lambda t}$. The minimum is $Y_1'$ when $Y_1' <
Y_j'$ for all $j \neq 1$; conditioning on $Y_1' = s$, this has probability $\prod_{j \neq 1}e^{-\lambda_js} = e^{-(\Lambda -
\lambda_1)s}$, so $\mathbb P(Y_1' \text{ is the minimum}) = \int_0^\infty\lambda_1e^{-\lambda_1s}e^{-(\Lambda - \lambda_1)s}\,ds
= \lambda_1/\Lambda$ (ties have probability zero), and likewise for every $j$.

(3) For $n = 1$, $f_1(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}$. If (3) holds for $n$, then since $a_{n+1} = a_n + Y_{n+1}$ with $Y_{n+1}$
independent of $a_n$, the density of $a_{n+1}$ is the convolution
$$
f_{n+1}(t) = \int_0^tf_n(s)\,\lambda e^{-\lambda(t - s)}\,ds = \frac{\lambda^{n+1}e^{-\lambda t}}{(n - 1)!}\int_0^ts^{n-1}\,ds =
\frac{\lambda^{n+1}t^ne^{-\lambda t}}{n!} .
$$

(4) $N(t) = 0$ exactly when $Y_1 > t$, with probability $e^{-\lambda t}$. For $n \geq 1$, $N(t) = n$ exactly when $a_n \leq t <
a_n + Y_{n+1}$; since $Y_{n+1}$ is independent of $a_n$,
$$
\mathbb P(N(t) = n) = \int_0^tf_n(s)e^{-\lambda(t - s)}\,ds = \frac{\lambda^ne^{-\lambda t}}{(n - 1)!}\int_0^ts^{n-1}\,ds =
e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!},
$$
the [Poisson distribution](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution)
with mean $\lambda t$.

(5) The $Y_i$ are independent with mean $1/\lambda$ and finite fourth moments, so $a_n/n \to 1/\lambda$ with probability one
by the [strong law of large numbers](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#thm-strong-law-large-numbers),
and $a_n \to \infty$. Since $a_{N(t)} \leq t < a_{N(t)+1}$ and $N(t) \to \infty$,
$$
\frac{a_{N(t)}}{N(t)} \leq \frac t{N(t)} < \frac{a_{N(t)+1}}{N(t) + 1}\cdot\frac{N(t) + 1}{N(t)},
$$
and both ends tend to $1/\lambda$. $\square$

Two further facts are used below and are stated as quoted. The counts of a Poisson process in disjoint intervals are
independent ("independent increments"), so that the three-condition definition and the one above agree
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 2.2.2, pp. 77-78]; and the superposition of independent Poisson processes of rates
$\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ "is a Poisson process with parameter $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$" (*ibid.*, p. 78), of which part (2) is the
first arrival. Part (5) is the hypothesis on arrivals of Little's law.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The memoryless property of part (1) says that the time already waited carries no information. For arrivals it means that a
quiet interval does not make the next arrival due.

::: {#exm-pois-no-memory}
#### Nothing is due

A feed server receives requests as a Poisson process of rate $\lambda = 1192$ per second. If no request has arrived for
$5\,\mathrm{ms}$, the time to the next one is still $\operatorname{Exp}(1192)$, with mean $0.84\,\mathrm{ms}$, by part (1); the
