same holds for a service time already in progress, which is why the residual service of an exponential server is again
exponential.
:::

Part (4) gives the probability of an idle millisecond. It is not small.

::: {#exm-pois-idle-ms}
#### An empty millisecond

At $\lambda = 1192$ per second, a given millisecond contains no request with probability $\mathbb P(N(0.001) = 0) = e^{-1.192}
= 0.30$, and five or more with probability $0.034$, by part (4). Arrivals at a constant average rate are irregular on the
scale of a service time, and the irregularity is what makes requests wait.
:::

Many independent users produce Poisson arrivals. Superposition is the reason.

::: {#exm-pois-many-users}
#### Many independent users

Each of the photo service's users requests a feed page now and then, independently of the others. If each user's requests
were a Poisson process, their superposition would be one of rate $\sum\lambda_j$ by the quoted superposition property; for
users that are not Poisson themselves, the merged stream of many rare, independent users is still close to Poisson,
which is the Poisson limit for Bernoulli trials of
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#thm-poisson-limit)
applied to short time slots.
:::

Part (2) decides which event comes first. In a queue the competition is between an arrival and a completion.

::: {#exm-pois-competition}
#### Arrival or completion

In a single-server queue with arrivals at rate $\lambda$ and exponential service at rate $\mu$, while a request is in service
the next event is an arrival with probability $\lambda/(\lambda + \mu)$ and a completion with probability $\mu/(\lambda + \mu)$,
after a time $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda + \mu)$, by parts (1) and (2) [@zukerman2013introduction, Ch. 6, p. 130]. For a feed
server, the next event is an arrival with probability $1192/3192 = 0.37$.
:::

Part (4) also gives the spread of the count in a second. It matches the random assignment of the previous chapter.

::: {#exm-pois-count-spread}
#### Requests in a second

With $\lambda = 1192$ per second, $N(1) \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(1192)$, with mean $1192$ and standard deviation
$\sqrt{1192} = 34.5$, almost the binomial spread $34.4$ of @exm-lbr-feed: a server receiving a random share of a large stream
sees nearly Poisson counts.
:::

The interval between arrivals that contains a given instant is longer than average. Zukerman calls it a paradox.

::: {#exm-pois-inspection}
#### The inspection paradox

"If we pick a random point in time, the mean length of the interval between two consecutive Poisson occurrences must be
$1/\lambda + 1/\lambda = 2/\lambda$", because "if we pick a point of time at random we are likely to pick an interval that is
longer than the average" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 2.2.2, p. 78]. The run below repeats Zukerman's Homework 2.3 with a
fixed seed.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1.0, 20_000))                  # rate 1
points = rng.uniform(1, 10_000, 1000)
idx = np.searchsorted(a, points)                              # first arrival after each point
print(f"mean gap {np.diff(a).mean():.3f}; mean gap containing a random point {np.mean(a[idx] - a[idx - 1]):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean gap 0.987; mean gap containing a random point 1.979
```
:::

The Poisson process is the limit of the slot model of the previous chapter. The slots become infinitely short.

::: {#exm-pois-slots}
#### From slots to a process

The expiring cache of @prp-cdn-ttl-hit-ratio assumed a request in each slot of length $\delta$ with probability $p = \lambda\delta$.
The number of requests in time $t$ is then $\operatorname{Bin}(t/\delta, \lambda\delta)$, which tends to
$\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ as $\delta \to 0$, part (4), by the Poisson limit; the gap between requests, geometric in
slots, tends to $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$. The slot model was a Poisson process in discrete time.
:::

Part (3) gives the time until a batch of requests has accumulated. A server that processes requests in batches of ten waits
for it.

::: {#exm-pois-batch-wait}
#### Waiting for ten requests

A server that collects ten feed requests before processing them as one batch waits for $a_{10}$, which by part (3) has the Erlang
density with $n = 10$ and $\lambda = 1192$ per second: mean $10/1192 = 8.4\,\mathrm{ms}$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{10}/1192 =
2.7\,\mathrm{ms}$. The first request of each batch waits all of it, the last none: batching trades a predictable delay for
throughput, and the delay is set by the arrival rate, not by the server.
:::

Bursts occur even at a constant rate. Part (4) gives their frequency.

::: {#exm-pois-bursts}
#### Bursts without a cause

With $11.9$ requests per $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ on average, a window of $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ holds $25$ or more requests with probability
$\mathbb P(\operatorname{Poisson}(11.92) \geq 25) \approx 0.0006$, computed below. At $100$ such windows per second, a
burst of twice the average happens about every sixteen seconds with no cause at all.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
m = 11.92
tail = 1 - sum(exp(-m + k * log(m) - lgamma(k + 1)) for k in range(25))
print(f"P(N >= 25) = {tail:.5f}; such windows per second at 100 windows/s: {100 * tail:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(N >= 25) = 0.00063; such windows per second at 100 windows/s: 0.063
```
:::

Not every stream is Poisson. Synchronised clients are the common exception.

::: {#exm-pois-not-poisson}
#### When arrivals are not Poisson

A million phones that refresh at the top of every minute, or batch jobs started by a scheduler at midnight, send their
requests together: the counts in disjoint intervals are far from independent, and the burst at the full minute is much
larger than any Poisson burst of the same mean. Dean and Barroso's remedy for synchronised background activity is the
reverse, to synchronise it deliberately so that it disturbs only short windows [@dean2013tail, p. 77]. The models of this
section then apply between the bursts, not across them.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks part (1) on a sample. Conditioning on a long wait leaves the remaining wait unchanged.

::: {#exr-pois-no-memory}
#### Checking the lack of memory

From $10^6$ seeded $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ values, estimate $\mathbb P(Y > 1.5 \mid Y > 1)$ and $\mathbb P(Y > 0.5)$, and the mean of
$Y - 1$ given $Y > 1$. Do the same for a uniform law on $[0, 2]$ and say why the answers differ.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For the exponential law both probabilities are $e^{-0.5} = 0.607$ and the remaining mean is $1$, by part (1). For the uniform
law $\mathbb P(Y > 1.5 \mid Y > 1) = 0.5$ while $\mathbb P(Y > 0.5) = 0.75$, and the remaining mean is $0.5$: a uniform service
that has run for a while is closer to its end, and the exponential is the only law on $[0, \infty)$ with no such effect.

## Python

The two laws.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(15)
for name, y in (("exponential", rng.exponential(1.0, 10**6)), ("uniform[0,2]", rng.uniform(0, 2, 10**6))):
    print(f"{name:12s}: P(Y>1.5|Y>1) {np.mean(y[y > 1] > 1.5):.3f}, P(Y>0.5) {np.mean(y > 0.5):.3f}, "
          f"E[Y-1|Y>1] {np.mean(y[y > 1] - 1):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
exponential : P(Y>1.5|Y>1) 0.607, P(Y>0.5) 0.606, E[Y-1|Y>1] 0.998
uniform[0,2]: P(Y>1.5|Y>1) 0.499, P(Y>0.5) 0.749, E[Y-1|Y>1] 0.499
```
::::
:::

The second exercise applies part (2) to three servers that are all busy. The first to finish frees a place.

::: {#exr-pois-three-servers}
#### The first of three

Three busy servers have exponential service at rates $10$, $20$ and $30$ per second, and a fourth request is waiting. Give the
law of its waiting time and the probability that it is served by each server. Check by simulation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (1) the remaining service times are again $\operatorname{Exp}(10)$, $\operatorname{Exp}(20)$ and $\operatorname{Exp}(30)$,
and by part (2) the wait is $\operatorname{Exp}(60)$, mean $16.7\,\mathrm{ms}$, and the probabilities are $1/6$, $1/3$ and $1/2$.

## Python

A seeded check.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(16)
y = rng.exponential(1 / np.array([10, 20, 30]), size=(200_000, 3))
print(f"mean wait {y.min(axis=1).mean() * 1000:.2f} ms; shares {np.round(np.bincount(y.argmin(axis=1)) / len(y), 3)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean wait 16.71 ms; shares [0.167 0.332 0.501]
```
::::
:::

The third exercise compares simulated arrival times with part (3). The tenth arrival has an Erlang law.

::: {#exr-pois-erlang}
#### The tenth arrival

For a Poisson process of rate $\lambda = 2$, give the mean and variance of $a_{10}$ from part (3) and check $\mathbb P(a_{10} \leq 4)$
against $\mathbb P(N(4) \geq 10)$ from part (4), by formula and simulation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$a_{10}$ is a sum of ten independent $\operatorname{Exp}(2)$ variables: mean $5$, variance $10/4 = 2.5$. The events $\{a_{10} \leq
4\}$ and $\{N(4) \geq 10\}$ are the same, so $\mathbb P(a_{10} \leq 4) = 1 - \sum_{k < 10}e^{-8}8^k/k! = 0.283$.

## Python

The formula and a simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import exp, factorial
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
a10 = rng.exponential(0.5, size=(200_000, 10)).sum(axis=1)
poisson = 1 - sum(exp(-8) * 8**k / factorial(k) for k in range(10))
print(f"mean {a10.mean():.3f}, var {a10.var():.3f}; P(a10 <= 4) simulated {np.mean(a10 <= 4):.4f}, formula {poisson:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean 4.995, var 2.507; P(a10 <= 4) simulated 0.2851, formula 0.2834
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise checks part (4) by counting simulated arrivals. The counts in a unit of time should be Poisson.

::: {#exr-pois-counts}
#### Counting arrivals

Generate a Poisson process of rate $3$ over $10^5$ time units with a fixed seed, count the arrivals in each unit interval, and
compare the frequencies of $0, \dots, 6$ arrivals with $e^{-3}3^k/k!$. Compare also the variance of the counts with their mean.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The frequencies agree with the Poisson probabilities to about three decimals, and the variance equals the mean, $3$, as for
any Poisson law. A measured stream whose counts have a variance well above their mean is burstier than Poisson.

## Python

The frequencies and the two moments.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import exp, factorial
rng = np.random.default_rng(18)
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / 3, 400_000))
counts = np.bincount(a[a < 100_000].astype(int), minlength=100_000)
freq = np.bincount(counts, minlength=7)[:7] / len(counts)
print("observed", np.round(freq, 4)); print("Poisson ", np.round([exp(-3) * 3**k / factorial(k) for k in range(7)], 4))
print(f"mean {counts.mean():.3f}, variance {counts.var():.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
observed [0.0504 0.1498 0.2232 0.2213 0.1686 0.1024 0.05  ]
Poisson  [0.0498 0.1494 0.224  0.224  0.168  0.1008 0.0504]
mean 3.004, variance 3.025
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise proves that randomly selecting requests from a Poisson stream gives Poisson counts. Uploads are a
fraction of all requests.

::: {#exr-pois-thinning}
#### Selecting a fraction

Each request of a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ is independently an upload with probability $p$. Prove that the number of
uploads in $[0, t]$ is $\operatorname{Poisson}(p\lambda t)$, and give the probability of no upload in a second for the photo
service, where uploads are $694$ of $1.75 \times 10^5$ requests per second.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Given $N(t) = n$, the number of uploads $K$ is $\operatorname{Bin}(n, p)$. By part (4),
$$
\mathbb P(K = k) = \sum_{n \geq k}e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}\binom nkp^k(1 - p)^{n-k} = e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(p\lambda
t)^k}{k!}\sum_{m \geq 0}\frac{((1 - p)\lambda t)^m}{m!} = e^{-p\lambda t}\frac{(p\lambda t)^k}{k!}.
$$
With $p\lambda = 694$ per second, a second without uploads has probability $e^{-694}$, which is zero for all purposes.

## Python

A seeded check of the thinned counts.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
lam, p, t = 50.0, 0.1, 1.0
n = rng.poisson(lam * t, 200_000)
k = rng.binomial(n, p)
print(f"thinned counts: mean {k.mean():.3f}, variance {k.var():.3f} (Poisson({p * lam * t}) has both {p * lam * t})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
thinned counts: mean 4.996, variance 5.010 (Poisson(5.0) has both 5.0)
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise computes the probability of a burst within one service time. It is the event that makes requests queue.

::: {#exr-pois-burst-service}
#### A burst within a service time

A feed server receives $\lambda = 1192$ requests per second and takes $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ per request. Give the probability that at
least two more requests arrive during one service time, and the number of such service times per second when the server is
busy $60\%$ of the time.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The count in $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ is $\operatorname{Poisson}(0.596)$, so $\mathbb P(N \geq 2) = 1 - e^{-0.596}(1 + 0.596) = 0.121$.
There are $1192$ service times per second, so about $144$ of them see two or more arrivals: queues form constantly, even far
below capacity.

## Python

The probability and the count.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp
m = 1192 * 0.0005
p2 = 1 - exp(-m) * (1 + m)
print(f"P(N >= 2) = {p2:.4f}; per second {1192 * p2:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(N >= 2) = 0.1206; per second 144
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise looks at the longest gap between arrivals. Gaps of several times the mean occur among many.

::: {#exr-pois-longest-gap}
#### The longest gap

Among $n$ independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ gaps, prove that the longest exceeds $t$ with probability $1 - (1 -
e^{-\lambda t})^n$, and give the median of the longest gap among the $1192$ gaps of one second at $\lambda = 1192$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The longest is at most $t$ when every gap is, with probability $(1 - e^{-\lambda t})^n$ by independence; this is the fan-out
rule of @prp-fan-out-tail applied to gaps. Its median solves $(1 - e^{-\lambda t})^n = 1/2$, $t = -\log(1 - 2^{-1/n})/\lambda$:
for $n = \lambda = 1192$, $t = 6.3\,\mathrm{ms}$, $7.5$ times the mean gap.

## Python

The median and a seeded check.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import log
lam = n = 1192
median = -log(1 - 2 ** (-1 / n)) / lam
rng = np.random.default_rng(20)
sim = np.median(rng.exponential(1 / lam, size=(20_000, n)).max(axis=1))
print(f"median longest gap {median * 1000:.2f} ms (simulated {sim * 1000:.2f} ms), {median * lam:.1f} mean gaps")
```

```{.text .run-output}
median longest gap 6.25 ms (simulated 6.26 ms), 7.5 mean gaps
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise estimates a rate from a count. Part (4) gives the uncertainty.

::: {#exr-pois-rate-estimate}
#### Estimating the rate

A server counts $N = 4900$ requests in $5\,\mathrm{s}$. Estimate $\lambda$ and give an approximate $95\%$ interval, using that a
Poisson count has variance equal to its mean.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\hat\lambda = 4900/5 = 980$ per second. The count's standard deviation is about $\sqrt{4900} = 70$, so the interval for
$\lambda$ is $(4900 \pm 1.96 \times 70)/5$, that is $[953, 1007]$ per second: a $5\,\mathrm{s}$ window measures the rate to within
about $3\%$.

## Python

The interval.

```{.python .run}
from math import sqrt
N, t = 4900, 5.0
print(f"lambda = {N / t:.0f}/s, 95% interval [{(N - 1.96 * sqrt(N)) / t:.0f}, {(N + 1.96 * sqrt(N)) / t:.0f}]")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lambda = 980/s, 95% interval [953, 1007]
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise merges two streams with part (2). The next request's kind is a competition.

::: {#exr-pois-next-kind}
#### Feed or upload next?

Feed requests arrive at $1.74 \times 10^5$ and uploads at $694$ per second, as independent Poisson processes. Give the law of the
time to the next request of either kind, the probability that it is an upload, and the expected number of feed requests
between two uploads.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (2) the next request comes after $\operatorname{Exp}(174\,694)$, mean $5.7\,\mu\mathrm s$, and is an upload with
probability $694/174\,694 = 0.0040$. By part (1) the kinds of successive requests are independent with this probability, so
the number of feed requests between uploads is geometric with mean $1.74 \times 10^5/694 = 251$.

## Python

The three numbers.

```{.python .run}
feed, up = 1.74e5, 694
print(f"mean gap {1e6 / (feed + up):.2f} us; P(upload) {up / (feed + up):.4f}; feed requests between uploads {feed / up:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean gap 5.72 us; P(upload) 0.0040; feed requests between uploads 251
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise computes the mean of the interval that contains a fixed time $t$. It explains the inspection paradox.

::: {#exr-pois-paradox-formula}
#### The interval around a point

Using the independence of increments quoted after the proof, the time back from $t$ to the last arrival is $\min(t, Y)$ and the
time forward to the next is $Y'$, with $Y, Y'$ independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$. Compute the mean length of the
interval containing $t$, and its limit as $t \to \infty$. Compare with a simulation at $t = 1$ and $t = 100$, $\lambda = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\mathbb E[\min(t, Y)] = \int_0^t e^{-\lambda s}\,ds = (1 - e^{-\lambda t})/\lambda$ and $\mathbb E[Y'] = 1/\lambda$, so the mean
length is $(2 - e^{-\lambda t})/\lambda$, which tends to $2/\lambda$, Zukerman's value. At $t = 1$ it is $1.632$; at $t = 100$,
$2.000$.

## Python

The formula and a simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import exp
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
for t in (1.0, 100.0):
    a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1.0, size=(20_000, 400)), axis=1)
    after = (a > t).argmax(axis=1)
    rows = np.arange(len(a))
    before = np.where(after > 0, a[rows, after - 1], 0.0)
    print(f"t = {t:5.0f}: simulated {np.mean(a[rows, after] - before):.3f}, formula {2 - exp(-t):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t =     1: simulated 1.630, formula 1.632
t =   100: simulated 1.996, formula 2.000
```
::::
:::
::::

### The M/M/1 queue

Kendall's notation names a queue by its arrival process, its service-time distribution and its number of servers; in M/M/1
"M" means "Markovian - Poisson for the arrival process or Exponential for the service time distribution", and the queue has
"an infinite buffer and FIFO service order" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 3.1, p. 106]. With exponential services and
Poisson arrivals, the number of requests present is a birth-death process: it rises by one at rate $\lambda$ and falls by one
at rate $\mu$ when the server is busy. The theorem takes that fact, and two others from the theory of Markov processes, as
quoted, and derives everything else.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-mm1}
#### The M/M/1 queue

Let requests arrive as a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ at a single server with unlimited waiting room, which serves them
in order of arrival with service times that are independent, $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ and independent of the arrivals; let
$\rho = \lambda/\mu$. Take as quoted from @zukerman2013introduction [Ch. 6, p. 130, and Sec. 3.8, p. 114] that the number
$Q(t)$ in the system is a birth-death process with rates $b_n = \lambda$ and $d_n = \mu$; that when a stationary distribution
exists, long-run averages over time and over requests equal the stationary means; and that Poisson arrivals see the stationary
distribution (PASTA). Then:

(a) a stationary distribution exists if and only if $\rho < 1$, and it is $\pi_n = (1 - \rho)\rho^n$, $n \geq 0$;

(b) the server's utilisation is $1 - \pi_0 = \rho$, and $L = \rho/(1 - \rho)$, $L_q = \rho^2/(1 - \rho)$;

(c) $W = 1/(\mu - \lambda)$ and $W_q = \rho/(\mu - \lambda)$;

(d) the response time $T$ of a request in steady state is $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu - \lambda)$: $\mathbb P(T > t) = e^{-(\mu -
\lambda)t}$, and its $q$-quantile is $t_q = \log\bigl(1/(1 - q)\bigr)/(\mu - \lambda)$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) By the stationary law of
[birth-death processes](../../complexity-science/random-processes/index.qmd#prp-birth-death), a stationary distribution exists
if and only if $\mathcal Z = \sum_{n \geq 0}\prod_{k = 1}^nb_{k-1}/d_k = \sum_{n \geq 0}\rho^n$ is finite, that is $\rho < 1$,
and then $\pi_n = \rho^n/\mathcal Z = (1 - \rho)\rho^n$.

(b) The server is idle exactly when $Q = 0$, so its utilisation is $1 - \pi_0 = \rho$. Next, $L = \sum_{n \geq 0}n(1 - \rho)\rho^n =
(1 - \rho)\rho\sum_{n \geq 1}n\rho^{n-1} = (1 - \rho)\rho/(1 - \rho)^2 = \rho/(1 - \rho)$, differentiating the geometric series
term by term inside its radius of convergence. The number waiting is $Q - 1$ when $Q \geq 1$ and $0$ otherwise, so $L_q = L -
(1 - \pi_0) = \rho/(1 - \rho) - \rho = \rho^2/(1 - \rho)$.

(c) By Little's law (@thm-littles-law), whose hypotheses hold with the quoted equality of long-run and stationary means, and
whose arrival rate is $\lambda$ by part (5) of @def-poisson-process: $W = L/\lambda = 1/(\mu - \lambda)$ and $W_q = L_q/\lambda =
\rho/(\mu - \lambda)$.

(d) By PASTA an arriving request finds $n$ requests with probability $\pi_n$. Under FIFO it leaves when the $n$ requests ahead
of it and its own are done: the remaining service of the one in progress, which is $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ by part (1) of
@def-poisson-process, the $n - 1$ full services of those waiting and its own, so $T$ is a sum of $n + 1$ independent
$\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ variables, with the Erlang density $f_{n+1}$ of part (3). Hence $T$ has the density
$$
\sum_{n \geq 0}(1 - \rho)\rho^n\frac{\mu^{n+1}t^ne^{-\mu t}}{n!} = (1 - \rho)\mu e^{-\mu t}\sum_{n \geq 0}\frac{(\rho\mu t)^n}{n!} =
(\mu - \lambda)e^{-\mu t}e^{\lambda t} = (\mu - \lambda)e^{-(\mu - \lambda)t},
$$
which is $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu - \lambda)$. Solving $e^{-(\mu - \lambda)t} = 1 - q$ gives $t_q$. $\square$

The mean response time $W = (1/\mu)/(1 - \rho)$ is the service time divided by the idle fraction of the server: at $\rho = 0.5$ a
request takes twice its service time, at $0.9$ ten times, at $0.99$ a hundred times. This is the curve that load tests trace
out and that the chapter's figures show; its steep part is the knee. Part (d) adds that the percentiles scale the same way,
every one of them by the factor $1/(1 - \rho)$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example applies the theorem to a feed server. It explains what $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$ buys.

::: {#exm-mm1-feed-server}
#### A feed server

With $\lambda = 1192$ and $\mu = 2000$ per second, $\rho = 0.596$: $L = 1.48$ requests, $W = 1/808 = 1.24\,\mathrm{ms}$ against
a service time of $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$, and $t_{0.99} = \log 100/808 = 5.7\,\mathrm{ms}$. If the server modelled each feed request as
one exponential service, the planned utilisation of @exm-load-servers makes the mean response two and a half service times
and the p99 eleven and a half.
:::

@fig-mm1-response plots part (c) against the utilisation, with simulations at several loads. The curve leaves the
service time slowly and then turns up.

::: {#exm-mm1-figure}
#### The response-time curve

In @fig-mm1-response the mean response time in units of the service time is $1/(1 - \rho)$, and the p99 is $\log 100/(1 -
\rho)$; seeded simulations of the queue lie on both curves. The knee is not a point, but between $\rho = 0.7$ and $0.9$ the
mean triples.

![Mean and 99th-percentile response time of the M/M/1 queue in units of the mean service time, against the utilisation,
from the formulas (lines) and simulations (points).](figures/mm1_response.svg){#fig-mm1-response width=65%}
:::

Zukerman's first dimensioning problem asks for the slowest server that meets a mean delay. Part (c) solves it.

::: {#exm-mm1-dimension-mean}
#### Dimensioning for a mean

To meet a required mean delay $W_R$ at arrival rate $\lambda$, solve $W_R = 1/(\mu^* - \lambda)$: "$\mu^* = (1 + \lambda
E[D]_R)/E[D]_R$" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 6.9, p. 140]. For $\lambda = 1192$ and $W_R = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, $\mu^* = 2192$
per second; a server of $\mu = 2000$ cannot meet a $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ mean at this load.
:::

The percentile version uses part (d). Zukerman gives it too.

::: {#exm-mm1-dimension-percentile}
#### Dimensioning for a percentile

To have $\mathbb P(T > t) = e^{-(\mu^* - \lambda)t} \leq \alpha$, "$\mu^* = \lambda - \ln(\alpha)/t$"
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 6.12, p. 145]. For $p99 \leq 10\,\mathrm{ms}$ at $\lambda = 1192$: $\mu^* = 1192 + \log 100/0.01 =
1652$ per second, so $\mu = 2000$ meets it with room to spare.
:::

Faster servers carrying proportionally more load have shorter delays. Zukerman calls it the gain of multiplexing.

::: {#exm-mm1-multiplexing}
#### One fast server

"If the arrival rate increases from $\lambda$ to $N\lambda$ and we increase the service rate from $\mu$ to $N\mu$ (maintaining the
same $\rho$), the mean queue size and its distribution will remain the same. However ... it reduces by $N$ times to $1/[N(\mu -
\lambda)]$" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 6.11, p. 143]. By parts (b) and (c), $L$ depends only on $\rho$ while $W$ scales with
$1/\mu$: at the same utilisation, a server twice as fast has half the delay.
:::

Part (a) gives the probability of a long queue. It decays geometrically.

::: {#exm-mm1-long-queue}
#### A long queue

By part (a), $\mathbb P(Q \geq k) = \sum_{n \geq k}(1 - \rho)\rho^n = \rho^k$. At $\rho = 0.6$ a queue of ten or more occurs $0.6\%$
of the time; at $\rho = 0.9$, $35\%$ of the time. A buffer sized for ten requests overflows rarely at the first load and
constantly at the second.
:::

A discrete-event simulation checks the theorem and Little's law together. It is the chapter's main check of the formulas.

::: {#exm-mm1-simulation}
#### Simulating the queue

A SimPy simulation with $\lambda = 0.8$ and $\mu = 1$, seed $1$, records each request's response time and the time-average
number present; part (b) predicts $L = 4$, part (c) $W = 5$, and Little's law ties the measured $L$ to the measured $\lambda W$.

```{.python .run}
import simpy, numpy as np
LAM, MU, N = 0.8, 1.0, 100_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
env = simpy.Environment()
server = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=1)
times, area, last, inside = [], [0.0], [0.0], [0]
def change(delta):
    area[0] += inside[0] * (env.now - last[0]); last[0] = env.now; inside[0] += delta
def request():
    start = env.now; change(+1)
    with server.request() as r:
        yield r
        yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(1 / MU))
    change(-1); times.append(env.now - start)
def source():
    for _ in range(N):
        yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(1 / LAM))
        env.process(request())
env.process(source()); env.run()
L, W, lam = area[0] / env.now, np.mean(times), N / env.now
print(f"L = {L:.3f} (theory 4), W = {W:.3f} (theory 5), lambda*W = {lam * W:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
L = 4.103 (theory 4), W = 5.091 (theory 5), lambda*W = 4.103
```
:::

Zukerman also computes the delay of the requests that had to wait. It does not depend on the waiting probability.

::: {#exm-mm1-delayed}
#### Requests that wait

By PASTA a request waits with probability $\rho$; Little's law applied to the waiting room, with arrival rate $\lambda\rho$ of the
delayed requests, gives their mean wait "$E[\hat W_Q] = E[N_Q]/(\lambda\rho) = 1/(\mu - \lambda)$"
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 6.5, p. 134]. At $\rho = 0.6$ and $\mu = 2000$, $40\%$ of requests do not wait and the others
wait $1.25\,\mathrm{ms}$ on average.
:::

The curve's steepness makes the response time sensitive to small errors in the load. The previous chapter's error factors
enter here.

::: {#exm-mm1-sensitivity}
#### Ten percent more load

At $\rho = 0.5$ a $10\%$ increase of $\lambda$ raises $W$ from $2/\mu$ to $1/(0.45\mu) = 2.22/\mu$, by $11\%$. At $\rho = 0.9$ the same
increase gives $\rho = 0.99$ and $W$ rises from $10/\mu$ to $100/\mu$, tenfold. An estimate of the load known within $10\%$
(@prp-estimate-error) gives a response time known within $10\%$ at half load and not at all near capacity.
:::

The theorem gives the ratio between the p99 and the mean. It is the same at every load.

::: {#exm-mm1-p99-over-mean}
#### The p99 is 4.6 means

By parts (c) and (d), $t_{0.99}/W = \log 100 = 4.6$ for every $\rho < 1$. A measured ratio far above $4.6$ indicates a heavier
tail than the exponential model allows, for example a service time that is sometimes very long; a ratio below indicates more
regular service.
:::
::::

The first exercise tabulates parts (b) to (d). It shows how fast the queue grows near capacity.

::: {#exr-mm1-table}
#### The M/M/1 table

For $\mu = 2000$ per second and $\rho = 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95$, give $L$, $L_q$, $W$, $W_q$ and $t_{0.99}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By parts (b) to (d) with $\lambda = \rho\mu$; the table follows. Between $\rho = 0.8$ and $0.95$ the mean response time
quadruples, from $2.5$ to $10\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
from math import log
mu = 2000
print(" rho     L     Lq    W(ms)  Wq(ms)  p99(ms)")
for rho in (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95):
    lam = rho * mu
    print(f"{rho:4.2f} {rho / (1 - rho):6.2f} {rho**2 / (1 - rho):6.2f} {1000 / (mu - lam):7.2f} "
          f"{1000 * rho / (mu - lam):7.2f} {1000 * log(100) / (mu - lam):8.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
 rho     L     Lq    W(ms)  Wq(ms)  p99(ms)
0.50   1.00   0.50    1.00    0.50     4.61
0.70   2.33   1.63    1.67    1.17     7.68
0.80   4.00   3.20    2.50    2.00    11.51
0.90   9.00   8.10    5.00    4.50    23.03
0.95  19.00  18.05   10.00    9.50    46.05
```

The second exercise checks part (a) by a different route. The balance between neighbouring states gives the geometric law.

::: {#exr-mm1-balance}
#### The balance equations

Zukerman writes the global balance equations $\pi_0\lambda = \pi_1\mu$ and $\pi_i(\lambda + \mu) = \pi_{i+1}\mu + \pi_{i-1}\lambda$
for $i \geq 1$ [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 6.1, eq. (295)]. Prove by induction that they imply $\pi_i\lambda = \pi_{i+1}\mu$
for all $i \geq 0$, and deduce part (a).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For $i = 0$ it is the first equation. If $\pi_{i-1}\lambda = \pi_i\mu$, the equation for $i$ reads $\pi_i\lambda + \pi_i\mu =
\pi_{i+1}\mu + \pi_i\mu$, so $\pi_i\lambda = \pi_{i+1}\mu$. Then $\pi_n = \rho^n\pi_0$, and $\sum_n\pi_n = 1$ forces $\pi_0 = 1 -
\rho$ when $\rho < 1$ and has no solution otherwise.

## Python

The balance checked for the first states.

```{.python .run}
lam, mu = 0.8, 1.0
rho = lam / mu
pi = [(1 - rho) * rho**n for n in range(12)]
print("pi_0..pi_3:", [round(p, 4) for p in pi[:4]], "| sum of 12 terms", round(sum(pi), 4))
print("max balance error:", max(abs(pi[i] * (lam + mu) - pi[i + 1] * mu - pi[i - 1] * lam) for i in range(1, 11)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
pi_0..pi_3: [0.2, 0.16, 0.128, 0.1024] | sum of 12 terms 0.9313
max balance error: 2.7755575615628914e-17
```
::::
:::

The third exercise simulates the response-time distribution and compares it with part (d). The p99 is the test.

::: {#exr-mm1-distribution}
#### The law of the response time

Simulate an M/M/1 queue with $\lambda = 0.9$, $\mu = 1$ (seed $2$, $2 \times 10^5$ requests, discarding the first $10^4$), and compare
the empirical median, p90 and p99 of the response time with part (d).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (d) gives $t_q = \log(1/(1 - q))/0.1$: $6.9$, $23.0$ and $46.1$. The simulation agrees within a few percent; at $\rho = 0.9$
consecutive response times are strongly correlated, so $2 \times 10^5$ requests estimate the tail less precisely than
@prp-quantile-estimate would for independent samples.

## Python

A direct simulation by the recursion "start of service is the later of arrival and previous completion".

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n, lam, mu = 200_000, 0.9, 1.0
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / lam, n)); s = rng.exponential(1 / mu, n)
d = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    free = max(free, a[i]) + s[i]; d[i] = free
T = (d - a)[10_000:]
for q in (0.5, 0.9, 0.99):
    print(f"q = {q}: simulated {np.quantile(T, q):.2f}, theory {np.log(1 / (1 - q)) / (mu - lam):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
q = 0.5: simulated 6.89, theory 6.93
q = 0.9: simulated 23.65, theory 23.03
q = 0.99: simulated 48.55, theory 46.05
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise dimensions a server for a p99 with @exm-mm1-dimension-percentile. It also asks for the largest load.

::: {#exr-mm1-dimension}
#### A server for a p99

A shard receives $\lambda = 1192$ requests per second and must keep its p99 within $20\,\mathrm{ms}$. Give the slowest service rate
that meets it, and, for $\mu = 2000$, the largest arrival rate. Is the requirement feasible for any $\lambda$ if $\mu = 200$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (d), $\mu - \lambda \geq \log 100/0.02 = 230$: $\mu^* = 1422$ per second, and for $\mu = 2000$, $\lambda^* = 1770$ ($\rho =
0.885$). With $\mu = 200$ even $\lambda \to 0$ gives a p99 of $\log 100/200 = 23\,\mathrm{ms}$: the service time alone breaks the
requirement, Zukerman's infeasible case [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 6.12, p. 146].

## Python

The three answers.

```{.python .run}
from math import log
need = log(100) / 0.02
print(f"mu* = {1192 + need:.0f}/s; lambda* for mu = 2000: {2000 - need:.0f}/s; p99 at mu = 200, lambda -> 0: {log(100) / 200 * 1000:.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mu* = 1422/s; lambda* for mu = 2000: 1770/s; p99 at mu = 200, lambda -> 0: 23.0 ms
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise inverts part (c) for a target expressed in service times. It gives the largest utilisation.

::: {#exr-mm1-max-utilisation}
#### The largest utilisation

Prove that $W \leq k/\mu$ if and only if $\rho \leq 1 - 1/k$, and give the largest utilisation for mean response times of two,
five and ten service times. Which $k$ corresponds to the chapter-one choice $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$W = 1/(\mu(1 - \rho)) \leq k/\mu$ is equivalent to $1 - \rho \geq 1/k$. The largest utilisations are $0.5$, $0.8$ and $0.9$; and
$\rho_{\max} = 0.6$ corresponds to $k = 2.5$, a mean response of two and a half service times.

## Python

The utilisations.

```{.python .run}
for k in (2, 5, 10):
    print(f"W <= {k}/mu: rho <= {1 - 1 / k:.2f}")
print("k for rho = 0.6:", 1 / (1 - 0.6))
```

```{.text .run-output}
W <= 2/mu: rho <= 0.50
W <= 5/mu: rho <= 0.80
W <= 10/mu: rho <= 0.90
k for rho = 0.6: 2.5
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise derives the law of the waiting time before service. It has an atom at zero.

::: {#exr-mm1-wait-law}
#### The waiting time

Prove, with PASTA and FIFO, that the waiting time $T_q$ of a request in steady state satisfies $\mathbb P(T_q = 0) = 1 - \rho$ and
$\mathbb P(T_q > t) = \rho e^{-(\mu - \lambda)t}$ for $t \geq 0$, and check that its mean is $W_q$ of part (c).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A request that finds $0$ waits $0$, with probability $\pi_0 = 1 - \rho$. One that finds $n \geq 1$ waits for $n$ independent
$\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ services (the first a residual one), with density $f_n$. So for $t \geq 0$
$$
\mathbb P(T_q > t) = \sum_{n \geq 1}(1 - \rho)\rho^n\int_t^\infty f_n = \rho\int_t^\infty\sum_{m \geq 0}(1 - \rho)\rho^mf_{m+1}(s)\,ds
= \rho e^{-(\mu - \lambda)t},
$$
using the computation of part (d). The mean is $\int_0^\infty\rho e^{-(\mu - \lambda)t}\,dt = \rho/(\mu - \lambda) = W_q$.

## Python

The simulation of @exr-mm1-distribution, for the waiting time.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, lam, mu = 200_000, 0.9, 1.0
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / lam, n)); s = rng.exponential(1 / mu, n)
start = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    start[i] = max(free, a[i]); free = start[i] + s[i]
Tq = (start - a)[10_000:]
print(f"P(Tq = 0) {np.mean(Tq == 0):.3f} (theory {1 - lam / mu:.3f}); P(Tq > 10) {np.mean(Tq > 10):.3f} "
      f"(theory {0.9 * np.exp(-0.1 * 10):.3f}); mean {Tq.mean():.2f} (theory {0.9 / 0.1:.2f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(Tq = 0) 0.102 (theory 0.100); P(Tq > 10) 0.319 (theory 0.331); mean 9.11 (theory 9.00)
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise compares one server of rate $2\mu$ with two separate servers of rate $\mu$. Pooling halves the delay.

::: {#exr-mm1-split}
#### One fast server or two slow ones

Total traffic $\lambda$ is either split evenly between two M/M/1 queues of rate $\mu$ each, or sent to one server of rate $2\mu$.
Prove that the second has exactly half the mean response time of the first, and evaluate both for $\lambda = 3000$ and $\mu =
2000$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Each half is Poisson of rate $\lambda/2$ by thinning (@exr-pois-thinning), so each separate queue has $W = 1/(\mu - \lambda/2) =
2/(2\mu - \lambda)$; the fast server has $W = 1/(2\mu - \lambda)$, half as much, as in @exm-mm1-multiplexing. For $\lambda = 3000$:
$2\,\mathrm{ms}$ against $1\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The two means.

```{.python .run}
lam, mu = 3000, 2000
print(f"two separate: W = {1000 / (mu - lam / 2):.2f} ms; one fast: W = {1000 / (2 * mu - lam):.2f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
two separate: W = 2.00 ms; one fast: W = 1.00 ms
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise computes the variance of the number present. Near capacity the queue is not only long but erratic.

::: {#exr-mm1-variance}
#### How much the queue varies

Prove that $\operatorname{Var}(Q) = \rho/(1 - \rho)^2$, and give the standard deviation of $Q$ relative to its mean at $\rho = 0.6$
and $0.95$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$Q + 1$ is geometric with parameter $1 - \rho$ by part (a), whose variance is $\rho/(1 - \rho)^2$ by the moments of the
[geometric distribution](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution);
shifting by one does not change the variance. Relative to the mean $\rho/(1 - \rho)$, the standard deviation is
$1/\sqrt\rho$: $1.29$ at $0.6$ and $1.03$ at $0.95$. The queue's typical size and its fluctuations grow together.

## Python

The ratio, and the sample variance from a simulated stationary law.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
for rho in (0.6, 0.95):
    q = rng.geometric(1 - rho, 10**6) - 1
    print(f"rho = {rho}: var {q.var():.2f} (theory {rho / (1 - rho)**2:.2f}), sd/mean {q.std() / q.mean():.3f} "
          f"(theory {1 / np.sqrt(rho):.3f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
rho = 0.6: var 3.75 (theory 3.75), sd/mean 1.292 (theory 1.291)
rho = 0.95: var 380.66 (theory 380.00), sd/mean 1.026 (theory 1.026)
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise proves that a request waits with probability $\rho$. It is part (a) seen by an arrival.

::: {#exr-mm1-wait-probability}
#### The probability of waiting

Prove with PASTA that the fraction of requests that wait is $\rho$, and that the fraction that find at least $k$ others is
$\rho^k$. What fraction of feed requests waits at $\rho = 0.596$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By PASTA an arrival finds $n$ requests with probability $\pi_n$; it waits exactly when $n \geq 1$, with probability $1 - \pi_0 =
\rho$, and finds at least $k$ with probability $\sum_{n \geq k}\pi_n = \rho^k$ (@exm-mm1-long-queue). At $\rho = 0.596$, $59.6\%$ of
feed requests wait.

## Python

The fractions from the simulation recursion.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n, lam, mu = 200_000, 1192.0, 2000.0
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / lam, n)); s = rng.exponential(1 / mu, n)
start = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    start[i] = max(free, a[i]); free = start[i] + s[i]
print(f"fraction that waits {np.mean(start > a):.3f} (rho = {lam / mu:.3f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
fraction that waits 0.597 (rho = 0.596)
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise drops the exponential service time. Constant services wait less than the theorem predicts.

::: {#exr-mm1-constant-service}
#### Constant service times

Simulate a single server with Poisson arrivals at $\rho = 0.8$ and constant service times of $1$, and compare the mean waiting
time with $W_q$ of part (c) for exponential service of the same mean. Which assumption of the theorem fails, and in which
direction does it err?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The theorem assumes exponential service; with constant service $Q(t)$ is no longer a birth-death process. The simulated mean
wait is about $2$, half of the exponential $W_q = 4$: variability of service times causes waiting as much as variability of
arrivals, and the exponential law, with a standard deviation equal to its mean, is a pessimistic model of regular services and
an optimistic one of heavy-tailed ones.

## Python

The two simulations with the same arrivals.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 300_000
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / 0.8, n))
for name, s in (("constant", np.ones(n)), ("exponential", rng.exponential(1.0, n))):
    start = np.empty(n); free = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        start[i] = max(free, a[i]); free = start[i] + s[i]
    print(f"{name:11s}: mean wait {np.mean((start - a)[10_000:]):.2f}")
print("M/M/1 W_q at rho = 0.8:", 0.8 / (1 - 0.8))
```

```{.text .run-output}
constant   : mean wait 2.03
exponential: mean wait 4.14
M/M/1 W_q at rho = 0.8: 4.000000000000001
```
::::
:::
::::

## Multi-server queues and capacity planning {#sec-mmc}

A pool of servers fed from one queue behaves differently from the same servers with a queue each. While one server is busy
with a long request, another can take the next; requests wait only when all servers are busy. Zukerman's M/M/k model
captures this: "the M/M/k queue is a generalization of the M/M/1 queue to the case of k servers", fed by one Poisson stream
[@zukerman2013introduction, Ch. 9, p. 178]. Its central result, the Erlang C formula, gives the probability that a request
has to wait at all, and from it the mean wait and the number of servers a target requires. This section derives the model
completely, under the same quoted facts as the M/M/1 queue, and uses it to plan capacity.

For more on this topic, see @zukerman2013introduction [Ch. 9] and, for the practice of capacity and headroom,
@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 12, "Capacity and concurrency limits"].

### The M/M/c queue and Erlang C

With $c$ servers and $n$ requests present, $\min(n, c)$ servers are busy, so the number present falls at rate $\min(n, c)\mu$.
Below $c$ the queue behaves like $n$ independent servers; at $c$ and above, like one server of rate $c\mu$. The offered load
$a = \lambda/\mu$, in erlangs, is the mean number of servers the traffic would keep busy; the theorem holds when it is below
$c$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-erlang-c}
#### The M/M/c queue and the Erlang C formula

Let requests arrive as a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ at $c$ identical servers with one unlimited waiting room, served in
order of arrival by the first free server, with service times independent, $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ and independent of the
arrivals; let $a = \lambda/\mu$ and $\rho = a/c$. Take as quoted from @zukerman2013introduction [Sec. 9.1, p. 178, and Sec. 3.8]
that the number $Q(t)$ present is a birth-death process with rates $b_n = \lambda$ and $d_n = \min(n, c)\mu$, and, as for
@thm-mm1, that long-run averages equal stationary means and that Poisson arrivals see the stationary distribution. Then:

(a) a stationary distribution exists if and only if $a < c$, and then
$$
\pi_n = \pi_0\frac{a^n}{n!}\ (n < c), \qquad \pi_n = \pi_0\frac{a^n}{c!\,c^{n-c}}\ (n \geq c), \qquad \pi_0 = \Bigl(\sum_{n =
0}^{c-1}\frac{a^n}{n!} + \frac{a^c}{c!}\frac{c}{c - a}\Bigr)^{-1};
$$

(b) the probability that all servers are busy, which is the probability that an arriving request waits, is the **Erlang C
formula**
$$
C(c, a) = \sum_{n \geq c}\pi_n = \pi_0\frac{a^c}{c!}\frac{c}{c - a};
$$

(c) $L_q = C(c, a)\,\rho/(1 - \rho)$, $W_q = C(c, a)/(c\mu - \lambda)$, $W = W_q + 1/\mu$, the mean number of busy servers is $a$,
and the utilisation is $\rho$;

(d) the waiting time $T_q$ of a request in steady state satisfies $\mathbb P(T_q > t) = C(c, a)\,e^{-(c\mu - \lambda)t}$ for $t
\geq 0$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) By the stationary law of
[birth-death processes](../../complexity-science/random-processes/index.qmd#prp-birth-death), the products $\prod_{k = 1}^nb_{k-1}/d_k$
are $\lambda^n/(n!\mu^n) = a^n/n!$ for $n \leq c$ and $\frac{a^c}{c!}\rho^{n-c}$ for $n \geq c$. Their sum $\mathcal Z$ is finite if
and only if the geometric tail $\sum_{n \geq c}\frac{a^c}{c!}\rho^{n-c}$ converges, that is $\rho < 1$, or $a < c$; the tail is then
$\frac{a^c}{c!}\frac1{1 - \rho} = \frac{a^c}{c!}\frac c{c - a}$, which gives $\pi_0 = 1/\mathcal Z$ and $\pi_n = \pi_0\prod_k b_{k-1}/d_k$.

(b) Summing $\pi_n$ over $n \geq c$ gives the tail just computed times $\pi_0$. All servers are busy exactly when $Q \geq c$, and by
PASTA an arrival finds $Q \geq c$ with probability $C(c, a)$.

(c) Write $\pi_{c+j} = \pi_c\rho^j$, so that $C(c, a) = \pi_c/(1 - \rho)$. The number waiting is $(Q - c)^+$, and
$$
L_q = \sum_{j \geq 0}j\pi_c\rho^j = \pi_c\frac{\rho}{(1 - \rho)^2} = C(c, a)\frac{\rho}{1 - \rho} .
$$
By Little's law (@thm-littles-law) for the waiting room, $W_q = L_q/\lambda = C(c, a)\rho/(\lambda(1 - \rho))$, and $\rho/(\lambda(1 -
\rho)) = 1/(c\mu - \lambda)$. Applied to the servers, whose stay is a service time, the law gives a mean number in service of
$\lambda/\mu = a$, so $W = W_q + 1/\mu$ and the utilisation of each server, by symmetry the average, is $a/c = \rho$.

(d) A request that finds $c + j$ requests ($j \geq 0$) waits until $j + 1$ services end, all $c$ servers being busy throughout.
While $c$ servers are busy, by parts (1) and (2) of @def-poisson-process the time to the next completion is the minimum of $c$
independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ residual services, $\operatorname{Exp}(c\mu)$, and after each completion the residual
services of the others are again $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$; so the wait is a sum of $j + 1$ independent $\operatorname{Exp}(c\mu)$
variables. By PASTA, given that it waits, $j$ has probability $\pi_{c+j}/C(c, a) = (1 - \rho)\rho^j$, which is the law of the
number found by an arrival at an M/M/1 queue of service rate $c\mu$ and utilisation $\rho$. The computation of part (d) of
@thm-mm1 with $\mu$ replaced by $c\mu$ shows that, given that it waits, $T_q \sim \operatorname{Exp}(c\mu(1 - \rho)) =
\operatorname{Exp}(c\mu - \lambda)$. Hence $\mathbb P(T_q > t) = C(c, a)e^{-(c\mu - \lambda)t}$. $\square$

For $c = 1$ the theorem is @thm-mm1: $C(1, a) = a = \rho$ and $W_q = \rho/(\mu - \lambda)$. The new feature for large $c$ is that
$C(c, a)$ can be small even at high utilisation: many servers sharing one queue are rarely all busy at once, so most requests
do not wait, and the knee of the response-time curve moves towards $\rho = 1$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Two servers give the simplest new case. Zukerman's homework works it out.

::: {#exm-mmc-two-servers}
#### Two servers

For $c = 2$, part (a) gives $\pi_0 = (1 + a + a^2/(2 - a))^{-1} = (2 - a)/(2 + a)$ and part (b) $C(2, a) = a^2/(2 + a)$, as in
[@zukerman2013introduction, Homework 9.9]. At $a = 1$ ($\rho = 0.5$) a request waits with probability $1/3$, against $1/2$ at a
single server of the same utilisation.
:::

Zukerman tabulates Erlang C for large systems near capacity. The probability of waiting stays moderate at utilisations a
single server could not sustain.

::: {#exm-mmc-zukerman-table}
#### Large systems near capacity

Zukerman's table gives $C_k(A) = 0.025$ for $A = 20$, $k = 30$; $0.064$ for $A = 100$, $k = 117$; $0.158$ for $A = 500$, $k = 527$;
and $0.262$ for $A = 1000$, $k = 1029$ [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 9.2, p. 180]. With $1029$ servers at $97\%$ utilisation,
three requests in four do not wait at all.
:::

The feed tier of the running example is an M/M/c queue if its balancer sends each request to a free server. The probability
of waiting is then negligible.

::: {#exm-mmc-feed-tier}
#### The feed tier as one queue

With $\lambda = 1.74 \times 10^5$, $\mu = 2000$ and $c = 146$, the offered load is $a = 87$ erlangs and $\rho = 0.596$. The run
below gives $C(146, 87)$ of order $10^{-9}$: almost no request waits. The same servers as $146$ separate M/M/1 queues at
$\rho = 0.596$ would make $59.6\%$ of requests wait (@exr-mm1-wait-probability). A balancer that tracks free servers, such as
least connections, turns separate queues into a shared one, which is part of why it beats random assignment in
@fig-lb-algorithms.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    s = sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m)
    return exp(tail - m) / s
print(f"C(146, 87) = {erlang_c(146, 87):.2e}; C(1, 0.596) = {erlang_c(1, 0.596):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
C(146, 87) = 5.12e-09; C(1, 0.596) = 0.596
```
:::

Capacity planning asks for the fewest servers that meet a target. Zukerman's dimensioning problem uses part (b).

::: {#exm-mmc-dimension}
#### The fewest servers for a target

"One could solve the dimensioning problem of finding, for a given $A$, the smallest $k$ such that $C_k(A)$ or the mean delay is
lower than a given value", using that "the value of $C_k(A)$ decreases as $k$ increases" [@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 9.5,
p. 182]. For the feed's $a = 87$ erlangs and the target $C \leq 0.05$, the third exercise below finds the smallest $c$: about
a hundred servers, against the $146$ that the utilisation rule $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$ gave.
:::

The spare capacity that a target needs grows slower than the load. Zukerman hints at a square root.

::: {#exm-mmc-square-root}
#### Spare capacity grows like a square root

Zukerman's hospital homework observes that "as $n$ grows with $\lambda_1$, $n - \lambda_1$ approaches $C\sqrt n$ for some constant
$C$" [@zukerman2013introduction, Homework 9.10, p. 184]. The run below finds the smallest $c$ with $C(c, a) \leq 0.05$ for growing
$a$: the spare servers $c - a$ divided by $\sqrt a$ stay near a constant, so the utilisation of a large pool can be much closer to
one than that of a small pool at the same quality.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log, sqrt
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
for a in (10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    c = int(a) + 1
    while erlang_c(c, a) > 0.05:
        c += 1
    print(f"a = {a:5d}: c = {c:5d}, spare {c - a:4d}, spare/sqrt(a) = {(c - a) / sqrt(a):.2f}, utilisation {a / c:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
a =    10: c =    17, spare    7, spare/sqrt(a) = 2.21, utilisation 0.588
a =   100: c =   119, spare   19, spare/sqrt(a) = 1.90, utilisation 0.840
a =  1000: c =  1056, spare   56, spare/sqrt(a) = 1.77, utilisation 0.947
a = 10000: c = 10175, spare  175, spare/sqrt(a) = 1.75, utilisation 0.983
```
:::

A database connection pool is a multi-server queue. Queries wait for a connection when all are in use.

::: {#exm-mmc-connection-pool}
#### Waiting for a connection

A server sends $400$ queries per second to a database through a pool of $c$ connections, each query holding a connection for
$10\,\mathrm{ms}$ on average, so $a = 4$ erlangs. With $c = 5$ connections, $\rho = 0.8$ and a query waits with probability
$C(5, 4) = 0.55$; with $c = 8$, $C(8, 4) = 0.07$. The pool's size, not the database, can be the bottleneck, and Little's law alone
(@exm-little-connections) does not show it.
:::

Zukerman's hospital exercise criticises proportional sizing. Half the load does not need half the servers.

::: {#exm-mmc-hospital}
#### Half the load, half the beds?

In Zukerman's homework, ICU stays last $2.5$ days on average, Hospital 2 receives $2$ patients a day and has $10$ beds, and
Hospital 1, which receives one patient a day, is given half the beds because it has "half the traffic load"; the reader is
asked "to evaluate and criticize their decision" [@zukerman2013introduction, Homework 9.10, pp. 183-184]. Hospital 2 has $a =
5$ and $c = 10$; Hospital 1 has $a = 2.5$ and $c = 5$. The run below gives their probabilities of waiting: the smaller hospital,
at the same utilisation, makes patients wait more than three times as often.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
print(f"Hospital 2: C(10, 5) = {erlang_c(10, 5):.4f}; Hospital 1: C(5, 2.5) = {erlang_c(5, 2.5):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Hospital 2: C(10, 5) = 0.0361; Hospital 1: C(5, 2.5) = 0.1304
```
:::

Utilisation is the mean number of busy servers divided by $c$. Zukerman obtains it by Little's law.

::: {#exm-mmc-utilisation}
#### Utilisation of a pool

"The utilization of an M/M/k queue is the ratio of the mean number of busy servers to $k$", that is "$\hat U = A/k$"
[@zukerman2013introduction, Sec. 9.6, p. 182]. It does not depend on whether requests wait; two pools with the same $a/c$ have
the same utilisation and very different waits.
:::

A simulation checks parts (b) and (c). The SimPy resource has $c$ servers and one queue.

::: {#exm-mmc-simulation}
#### Simulating M/M/5

With $\lambda = 4$, $\mu = 1$ and $c = 5$ (seed $3$), the fraction of requests that wait and the mean wait are compared with
$C(5, 4) = 0.554$ and $W_q = C/(c\mu - \lambda) = 0.554$.

```{.python .run}
import simpy, numpy as np
LAM, MU, C, N = 4.0, 1.0, 5, 100_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
env = simpy.Environment()
servers = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=C)
waits = []
def request():
    t0 = env.now
    with servers.request() as r:
        yield r
        waits.append(env.now - t0)
        yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(1 / MU))
def source():
    for _ in range(N):
        yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(1 / LAM))
        env.process(request())
env.process(source()); env.run()
w = np.array(waits[5000:])
print(f"P(wait) {np.mean(w > 0):.3f}, W_q {w.mean():.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(wait) 0.555, W_q 0.535
```
:::

@fig-mmc-erlang-c plots part (b) against the number of servers for three loads. Each curve falls steeply once $c$ exceeds $a$ by
a few servers.

::: {#exm-mmc-figure}
#### The probability of waiting

In @fig-mmc-erlang-c, $C(c, a)$ is one at $c \leq a$ (no stationary regime) and falls from near one to near zero within a few
multiples of $\sqrt a$ above $a$, as @exm-mmc-square-root found numerically; the mean response time falls with it to the service
time.

![Probability of waiting in the M/M/c queue against the number of servers, for offered loads of 10, 50 and 87
erlangs.](figures/mmc_erlang_c.svg){#fig-mmc-erlang-c width=65%}
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise reproduces Zukerman's table of @exm-mmc-zukerman-table. Large factorials need logarithms.

::: {#exr-mmc-table}
#### Reproducing the table

Compute $C(c, a)$ for $(a, c) = (20, 30), (100, 117), (500, 527), (1000, 1029), (5000, 5010)$ with part (b), working in logarithms,
and compare with Zukerman's values $0.025, 0.064, 0.158, 0.262, 0.835$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The terms $a^n/n!$ overflow floating point for $a$ in the hundreds, so each is computed as $\exp(n\log a - \log n!)$ after
subtracting the largest logarithm; the values agree with Zukerman's to the digits he gives.

## Python

The five values.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
for a, c, z in ((20, 30, 0.025), (100, 117, 0.064), (500, 527, 0.158), (1000, 1029, 0.262), (5000, 5010, 0.835)):
    print(f"a = {a:4d}, c = {c:4d}: C = {erlang_c(c, a):.3f} (Zukerman {z})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
a =   20, c =   30: C = 0.025 (Zukerman 0.025)
a =  100, c =  117: C = 0.064 (Zukerman 0.064)
a =  500, c =  527: C = 0.158 (Zukerman 0.158)
a = 1000, c = 1029: C = 0.263 (Zukerman 0.262)
a = 5000, c = 5010: C = 0.835 (Zukerman 0.835)
```
::::
:::

The second exercise proves the two-server formula of @exm-mmc-two-servers. It is part (a) for $c = 2$.

::: {#exr-mmc-two-proof}
#### Two servers, by hand

Prove that for $c = 2$ and $a < 2$, $\pi_0 = (2 - a)/(2 + a)$, $C(2, a) = a^2/(2 + a)$ and $L = 4a/(4 - a^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (a), $1/\pi_0 = 1 + a + \frac{a^2}2\cdot\frac2{2 - a} = \frac{(1 + a)(2 - a) + a^2}{2 - a} = \frac{2 + a}{2 - a}$. Then $C =
\pi_0\frac{a^2}{2 - a} = \frac{a^2}{2 + a}$. By part (c) with $\rho = a/2$, $L_q = C\frac{a/2}{1 - a/2} = \frac{a^3}{(2 + a)(2 -
a)}$, and $L = L_q + a = \frac{a^3 + a(4 - a^2)}{4 - a^2} = \frac{4a}{4 - a^2}$, Zukerman's result.

## Python

The formulas against the general computation at $a = 1.5$.

```{.python .run}
a = 1.5
pi0 = 1 / (1 + a + a**2 / 2 * 2 / (2 - a))
C = pi0 * a**2 / 2 * 2 / (2 - a)
print(f"pi0 {pi0:.4f} vs {(2 - a) / (2 + a):.4f}; C {C:.4f} vs {a**2 / (2 + a):.4f}; "
      f"L {C * (a / 2) / (1 - a / 2) + a:.4f} vs {4 * a / (4 - a**2):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
pi0 0.1429 vs 0.1429; C 0.6429 vs 0.6429; L 3.4286 vs 3.4286
```
::::
:::

The third exercise dimensions the feed tier for a waiting probability and for a mean wait. It completes @exm-mmc-dimension.

::: {#exr-mmc-dimension}
#### Dimensioning the feed tier

For $a = 87$ erlangs and $\mu = 2000$, find the smallest $c$ with $C(c, a) \leq 0.05$, and the smallest with $W_q \leq
0.1\,\mathrm{ms}$. Compare their utilisations with $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The targets need $104$ and $91$ servers, at utilisations $0.84$ and $0.96$; the rule $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$ asks for $146$, which
buys headroom for estimation errors and failures (@exr-lb-pool-headroom) rather than for queueing, which a shared queue
handles with far fewer servers.

## Python

The two searches.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
a, mu = 87.0, 2000.0
c1 = next(c for c in range(88, 300) if erlang_c(c, a) <= 0.05)
c2 = next(c for c in range(88, 300) if erlang_c(c, a) / (c * mu - a * mu) <= 1e-4)
print(f"C <= 0.05: c = {c1} (utilisation {a / c1:.3f}); W_q <= 0.1 ms: c = {c2} (utilisation {a / c2:.3f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
C <= 0.05: c = 104 (utilisation 0.837); W_q <= 0.1 ms: c = 91 (utilisation 0.956)
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise compares one shared queue with separate queues for the same servers. It quantifies @exm-mmc-feed-tier.

::: {#exr-mmc-pooling}
#### Shared or separate queues

Ten servers of $\mu = 100$ per second receive $\lambda = 800$ per second in total. Give $W_q$ when the stream is split evenly into
ten M/M/1 queues, and when the servers share one queue. By what factor does sharing reduce the mean wait?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Separately, each queue has $\rho = 0.8$ and $W_q = 0.8/(100 - 80) = 40\,\mathrm{ms}$. Shared, $a = 8$ and $C(10, 8) = 0.41$, so
$W_q = 0.41/(1000 - 800) = 2.05\,\mathrm{ms}$: twenty times less, with the same servers and the same utilisation.

## Python

The two waits.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
lam, mu, c = 800.0, 100.0, 10
separate = (lam / c / mu) / (mu - lam / c)
shared = erlang_c(c, lam / mu) / (c * mu - lam)
print(f"separate W_q {separate * 1000:.2f} ms, shared W_q {shared * 1000:.2f} ms, factor {separate / shared:.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
separate W_q 40.00 ms, shared W_q 2.05 ms, factor 19.6
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise checks part (d) by simulation. The tail of the wait is exponential after the atom at zero.

::: {#exr-mmc-wait-tail}
#### The tail of the wait

Simulate the M/M/5 queue of @exm-mmc-simulation with the recursion for $c$ servers (each request takes the server that frees
first), and compare $\mathbb P(T_q > t)$ for $t = 0, 0.5, 1, 2$ with $C(5, 4)e^{-(5 - 4)t}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Under FIFO with $c$ servers, request $i$ starts at the later of its arrival and the earliest time a server is free; keeping the
servers' free times in a heap gives the waits in one pass. The simulated tails agree with part (d) to two decimals.

## Python

The heap recursion.

```{.python .run}
import heapq, numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
n, lam, mu, c = 300_000, 4.0, 1.0, 5
a = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / lam, n)); s = rng.exponential(1 / mu, n)
free = [0.0] * c; waits = np.empty(n)
for i in range(n):
    f = heapq.heappop(free); start = max(f, a[i]); waits[i] = start - a[i]; heapq.heappush(free, start + s[i])
w = waits[10_000:]
C = 0.5541
for t in (0, 0.5, 1, 2):
    print(f"t = {t}: simulated {np.mean(w > t):.3f}, theory {C * np.exp(-(c * mu - lam) * t):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t = 0: simulated 0.549, theory 0.554
t = 0.5: simulated 0.329, theory 0.336
t = 1: simulated 0.197, theory 0.204
t = 2: simulated 0.073, theory 0.075
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise proves the number in service directly from part (a). Little's law gave it in one line.

::: {#exr-mmc-busy-servers}
#### Busy servers by summation

Prove from part (a) that $\mathbb E[\min(Q, c)] = a$, without Little's law.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The detailed balance of the birth-death process, $\pi_n\lambda = \pi_{n+1}\min(n + 1, c)\mu$ for all $n \geq 0$, summed over $n$,
gives $\lambda\sum_n\pi_n = \mu\sum_{n \geq 0}\min(n + 1, c)\pi_{n+1} = \mu\,\mathbb E[\min(Q, c)]$, since the term for $Q = 0$ is
zero. So $\mathbb E[\min(Q, c)] = \lambda/\mu = a$: the rate of completions, $\mu$ per busy server, balances the rate of arrivals.

## Python

The sum for $c = 5$, $a = 4$, truncated far in the tail.

```{.python .run}
from math import factorial
a, c = 4.0, 5
w = [a**n / factorial(n) if n < c else a**n / (factorial(c) * c**(n - c)) for n in range(400)]
pi0 = 1 / sum(w)
print(f"E[min(Q, c)] = {sum(min(n, c) * x * pi0 for n, x in enumerate(w)):.6f} (a = {a})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
E[min(Q, c)] = 4.000000 (a = 4.0)
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise dimensions for a percentile of the wait. Part (d) turns it into an equation.

::: {#exr-mmc-percentile}
#### A percentile of the wait

With $\mu = 100$ per second and $\lambda = 800$, find the smallest $c$ such that at most $1\%$ of requests wait more than $10\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (d) the condition is $C(c, 8)e^{-(100c - 800) \times 0.01} \leq 0.01$. At $c = 10$ the left side is $0.41e^{-2} = 0.055$;
the search below finds the smallest $c$ that brings it under $0.01$.

## Python

The search.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
lam, mu, t = 800.0, 100.0, 0.01
for c in range(9, 16):
    p = erlang_c(c, lam / mu) * exp(-(c * mu - lam) * t)
    print(f"c = {c}: P(T_q > 10 ms) = {p:.4f}")
    if p <= 0.01:
        break
```

```{.text .run-output}
c = 9: P(T_q > 10 ms) = 0.2403
c = 10: P(T_q > 10 ms) = 0.0554
c = 11: P(T_q > 10 ms) = 0.0122
c = 12: P(T_q > 10 ms) = 0.0026
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise balances the cost of servers against the cost of waiting. It is the trade-off behind every capacity plan.

::: {#exr-mmc-cost}
#### Servers against waiting

A server costs $1$ per hour, and each second of waiting by a request costs $0.0005$. With $\lambda = 800$ per second and $\mu = 100$,
find the $c$ that minimises the hourly cost $c + 0.0005 \times 3600\lambda W_q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The waiting cost per hour is $0.0005$ times the total waiting time of the $3600\lambda$ requests of an hour, $3600\lambda W_q$. At $c
= 9$ the waiting is long and costly; it falls steeply and the server cost rises linearly, so the minimum is at a small
excess over $a = 8$, found below.

## Python

The cost for each $c$.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
lam, mu = 800.0, 100.0
costs = {c: c + 0.0005 * 3600 * lam * erlang_c(c, lam / mu) / (c * mu - lam) for c in range(9, 16)}
for c, v in costs.items():
    print(f"c = {c}: cost {v:.2f}")
print("best c:", min(costs, key=costs.get))
```

```{.text .run-output}
c = 9: cost 18.41
c = 10: cost 12.95
c = 11: cost 12.18
c = 12: cost 12.50
c = 13: cost 13.22
c = 14: cost 14.09
c = 15: cost 15.04
best c: 11
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise computes Zukerman's hospital example of @exm-mmc-hospital for a range of sizes. The rule of thumb that
emerges is the square root.

::: {#exr-mmc-hospital-rule}
#### A staffing rule

Zukerman asks for the beds Hospital 1 needs to match Hospital 2's probability of waiting, $C(10, 5)$, when it receives $4,
8, 16, 32, 64$ patients a day with stays of $2.5$ days [@zukerman2013introduction, Homework 9.10, p. 184]. Find the smallest
$c$ for each, and fit the rule $c \approx a + \beta\sqrt a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The offered loads are $a = 2.5\lambda_1 = 10, \dots, 160$ erlangs. The required spare capacity $c - a$ grows roughly
proportionally to $\sqrt a$, so $(c - a)/\sqrt a$ stays near a constant $\beta$, printed below. This is the "simple rule" Zukerman's homework asks for, found here numerically and
not proved.

## Python

The smallest $c$ and the fitted constant.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log, sqrt
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
target = erlang_c(10, 5)
betas = []
for a in (10, 20, 40, 80, 160):
    c = next(c for c in range(a + 1, 4 * a + 10) if erlang_c(c, a) <= target)
    betas.append((c - a) / sqrt(a))
    print(f"a = {a:3d}: c = {c:3d}, (c - a)/sqrt(a) = {betas[-1]:.2f}")
print(f"target C = {target:.3f}; mean beta = {sum(betas) / len(betas):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
a =  10: c =  17, (c - a)/sqrt(a) = 2.21
a =  20: c =  30, (c - a)/sqrt(a) = 2.24
a =  40: c =  53, (c - a)/sqrt(a) = 2.06
a =  80: c =  98, (c - a)/sqrt(a) = 2.01
a = 160: c = 185, (c - a)/sqrt(a) = 1.98
target C = 0.036; mean beta = 2.10
```

:::

The tenth exercise models the cores of one server. A process with $c$ worker threads on $c$ cores is an M/M/c queue if requests
are exponential.

::: {#exr-mmc-cores}
#### Cores of one machine

A feed server has $8$ cores, each serving $250$ requests per second, so its capacity is $2000$ per second. At $1192$ requests per
second, compare its mean response time as an M/M/8 queue with that of the M/M/1 model of @exm-mm1-feed-server, which treated it
as one fast server.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

As one server of rate $2000$, $W = 1.24\,\mathrm{ms}$ with a service time of $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$. As eight cores of $250$, $a =
4.77$, and $W = W_q + 4\,\mathrm{ms}$ with a small $W_q$: the mean is much longer, because each request is served by one core at an
eighth of the speed. Which model fits depends on whether a request can use all the cores; pooling reduces waiting, but speed
reduces service time, and the fast single server of @exm-mm1-multiplexing has both.

## Python

The two means.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, lgamma, log
def erlang_c(c, a):
    logs = [n * log(a) - lgamma(n + 1) for n in range(c)]
    tail = c * log(a) - lgamma(c + 1) + log(c / (c - a))
    m = max(logs + [tail])
    return exp(tail - m) / (sum(exp(x - m) for x in logs) + exp(tail - m))
lam = 1192.0
w1 = 1 / (2000 - lam)
c, mu = 8, 250.0
w8 = erlang_c(c, lam / mu) / (c * mu - lam) + 1 / mu
print(f"M/M/1 at 2000/s: W = {w1 * 1000:.2f} ms; M/M/8 at 250/s per core: W = {w8 * 1000:.2f} ms "
      f"(W_q = {(w8 - 1 / mu) * 1000:.3f} ms)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
M/M/1 at 2000/s: W = 1.24 ms; M/M/8 at 250/s per core: W = 4.17 ms (W_q = 0.168 ms)
```
